A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: What causes SENILE ptosis?
opts: Interruption of the sympathetic supply
Sympathetic interruption causes Horner syndrome's ptosis; senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle, relaxed tissues and herniated fat.
Compression of the oculomotor nerve
Oculomotor damage is a separate ptosis cause; senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle, relaxed tissues and herniated fat.
Weakened muscle, relaxed tissues
Correct — senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle and relaxed tissues, plus the weight of herniated fat.
Antibody blockade at the neuromuscular junction
Myasthenia gravis is a separate cause of ptosis; senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle, relaxed tissues and herniated fat.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 29

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: Why is natural light preferred for inspecting the skin?
opts: Artificial light makes lesion borders appear larger than they are
Apparent lesion size is not the issue; artificial light is avoided because it may distort skin tone.
Natural light reduces the glare produced by moist lesions
Glare is not the concern; artificial light is avoided because it may distort skin tone, so natural light is preferred.
Artificial light may distort skin tone
Correct — the distortion can conceal jaundice, pallor and subtle erythema.
Natural light is brighter than any artificial source available in clinic
Brightness is not the reason; natural light is preferred because artificial light may distort skin tone.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Besides Horner syndrome and the senile and congenital forms, which causes of ptosis remain?
opts: Bell palsy, trigeminal neuralgia and stroke
None of these is a ptosis cause; drooping of the upper lid comes from myasthenia gravis or oculomotor nerve damage.
Thyroid eye disease, orbital cellulitis and tumor
Orbital disease such as cellulitis or tumor causes proptosis, not ptosis; ptosis comes from myasthenia gravis or third nerve damage.
Blepharitis, chalazion and dermatochalasis
Lid lesions such as a chalazion are not ptosis causes; the remaining causes are myasthenia gravis and oculomotor nerve damage.
Myasthenia gravis, oculomotor nerve damage
Correct — ptosis also comes from myasthenia gravis and oculomotor nerve damage, alongside Horner syndrome's sympathetic loss.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 29

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which description fits a typical tongue cancer?
opts: On the dorsum, as smooth red patches, in females under thirty
The dorsum and smooth red patches are wrong; cancers sit on the lateral border or undersurface, usually in males over 50.
At the tip, as painful ulcers, in any age group
Painful ulcers at the tip are more typical of aphthous ulceration.
On the undersurface, as blue tortuous swellings
Blue tortuous swellings under the tongue are varicose veins; cancer appears as an indurated red or white lesion.
On the lateral border or undersurface, as an indurated lesion
Correct. Tongue cancers are usually indurated red or white lesions on the lateral border or undersurface, typically in males over 50.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which medication history should be taken specifically when a patient reports hearing loss?
opts: Oral contraceptives and hormone replacement
Hormonal agents are not the ototoxic drugs to ask about; those are aminoglycosides, aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, quinine and furosemide.
Aminoglycosides
Correct. Aminoglycosides are ototoxic, as are aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, quinine and furosemide, so each is asked about by name.
Beta blockers, statins and proton pump inhibitors
These are not the ototoxic drugs to ask about; those are aminoglycosides, aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, quinine and furosemide.
Inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators
Respiratory agents are not the ototoxic drugs; those are aminoglycosides, aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, quinine and furosemide.

A.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
A.q: Generalized itching with no obvious skin lesion should prompt consideration of which causes?
opts: Contact dermatitis and scabies exclusively
Contact dermatitis and scabies are not among them; generalized itching points to dry skin, aging, pregnancy, uremia, jaundice, lymphomas, leukemias, drug reaction or lice.
Anxiety and stress, once organic causes have been excluded
Anxiety is not among them; the causes are dry skin, aging, pregnancy, uremia, jaundice, lymphomas, leukemias, drug reaction and lice.
Dry skin, aging, pregnancy, uremia, jaundice, lymphomas, leukemias, drug reaction and lice
Correct — the list spans dermatological, systemic, malignant and infestational causes.
Dry skin and aging only, since these account for nearly all cases
The differential is considerably broader and includes systemic disease.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: What are the pupil findings in Adie's tonic pupil?
opts: Small, unequal and irregular; no light reaction but constricts on accommodation
Small, irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light are the Argyll Robertson pupil; Adie's is large and regular.
Small but briskly reactive, with ptosis and anhidrosis
A small, briskly reactive pupil with ptosis and anhidrosis is Horner syndrome; Adie's pupil is large and regular.
Dilated and fixed to both light and near, with ptosis and lateral deviation
A dilated pupil fixed to light and near, with ptosis and lateral deviation, is oculomotor palsy; Adie's keeps a slow near reaction.
Large, regular, usually unilateral
Correct — Adie's pupil is large, regular and usually unilateral, with a reduced light reaction and a very slow near reaction.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 82

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What is the Rinne result in SENSORINEURAL hearing loss?
opts: The result is unpredictable in sensorineural loss
The result is predictable: in sensorineural loss air conduction still outlasts bone conduction, as it does normally.
Air conduction still greater than bone conduction
Correct. Air conduction stays longer than bone conduction and the normal pattern prevails, because the inner ear or cochlear nerve fails however the vibrations arrive.
Bone conduction greater than air conduction, because the inner ear is damaged
That is the conductive pattern; a damaged inner ear does not favor the bone route.
Neither route is heard
Sensorineural loss reduces hearing but does not usually abolish it.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which two symptoms together suggest an allergic cause?
opts: Deep pain and photophobia
Deep pain suggests acute narrow angle glaucoma and photophobia suggests iritis; itching with tearing suggests allergy.
Burning and purulent discharge
Purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection; itching with excessive tearing is what suggests an allergic cause.
Foreign body sensation and reduced vision
Those fit a corneal injury such as an abrasion; itching with excessive tearing is what suggests an allergic cause.
Itching and excessive tearing
Correct — itching together with excessive tearing suggests an allergic cause of the eye complaint.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 12

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: A smooth, beefy red tongue points to which deficiency?
opts: Vitamin B12
Correct. The appearance is atrophic glossitis, and it earns a look for the rest of the deficiency picture.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C deficiency affects the gums rather than the tongue surface; the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to B12.
Iron alone
Iron deficiency has its own oral signs, but the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to vitamin B12.
Vitamin D
Vitamin D deficiency is not the cause; a smooth, beefy red tongue is the sign of vitamin B12 deficiency.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: Which part of the hand should be used to assess skin temperature?
opts: The ulnar border
The ulnar border is used to assess vibration in some examinations, not temperature.
The dorsal aspect
Correct — the back of the hand is more sensitive to temperature than the palm.
The palmar aspect
The palm is used for texture and vibration rather than temperature.
The fingertips
Fingertips are best for fine tactile discrimination, not temperature.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Eye pain ON EYE MOTION suggests what?
opts: Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis pairs eye pain with a gritty feeling; pain on eye motion suggests optic neuritis.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Acute narrow angle glaucoma pairs eye pain with headache; pain on eye motion suggests optic neuritis.
Optic neuritis
Correct — eye pain that comes with eye motion is the pairing for optic neuritis.
Corneal abrasion
A corneal abrasion hurts with blinking; pain on eye motion suggests optic neuritis.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 17

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which statement correctly sorts migraine, tension and cluster headaches by their EPISODIC and UNILATERAL patterns?
opts: Migraine and cluster are episodic; migraine and tension are unilateral
The pairings are swapped: migraine and tension are episodic, while migraine and cluster are unilateral.
All three are episodic and all three unilateral
Not all three share both features: migraine and tension are episodic, and migraine and cluster are unilateral.
Only cluster is episodic and only tension unilateral
Cluster is not the only episodic one, and tension is episodic, not unilateral; migraine and cluster are unilateral.
Migraine and tension are episodic; migraine and cluster are unilateral
Correct. Migraine appears in both lists, which is why the two features have to be taken together rather than either alone.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What does tracheal DEVIATION suggest?
opts: Thyroid nodules only
A mass may deviate the trachea, but so can atelectasis or a large pneumothorax, not only thyroid nodules.
Lymphadenopathy
Lymphadenopathy is not a cause of deviation; tracheal deviation suggests masses, atelectasis or a large pneumothorax.
Ludwig's angina
That threatens the airway by swelling of the floor of the mouth rather than by deviating the trachea.
Masses, atelectasis or a large pneumothorax
Correct. Something is either pulling the trachea toward it or pushing it away.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Eye pain with PHOTOPHOBIA suggests what?
opts: Inflammation of the iris
Correct — eye pain accompanied by photophobia is the pairing for inflammation of the iris.
Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis causes pain on eye motion; eye pain with photophobia suggests inflammation of the iris.
Temporal arteritis
Temporal arteritis pairs eye pain with temporal pain; photophobia suggests inflammation of the iris.
Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis pairs eye pain with a gritty feeling; photophobia suggests inflammation of the iris.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 17

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: What is trichiasis?
opts: Inward turning of the lower lid margin
An in-turned lower lid margin is entropion; trichiasis is posteriorly misdirected eyelashes.
Outward turning of the lower lid margin
An out-turned lower lid margin is ectropion, common in the elderly; trichiasis is posteriorly misdirected eyelashes.
Drooping of the upper lid
Drooping of the upper lid is ptosis; trichiasis is posteriorly misdirected eyelashes.
Posteriorly misdirected eyelashes
Correct — trichiasis is posteriorly misdirected eyelashes, a lid finding separate from entropion and ectropion.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 35

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: VERTICAL diplopia — images on top of each other — points to a palsy of which cranial nerves?
opts: Third or sixth
Third or sixth nerve palsy gives HORIZONTAL diplopia, images side by side; vertical points to III or IV.
Fourth or sixth
The sixth nerve belongs to the horizontal pattern; vertical diplopia points to a palsy of cranial nerve III or IV.
Second or third
The second nerve is the optic nerve, carrying the afferent visual signal; vertical diplopia points to III or IV.
Third or fourth
Correct — vertical diplopia, with images on top of each other, points to a palsy of cranial nerve III or IV.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 18

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: How is the whispered voice test set up?
opts: Stand beside the patient and whisper into both ears at once
Each ear is tested on its own with the other occluded, whispering from two feet behind the patient.
Stand two feet behind the patient, occlude the ear not being tested
Correct. The examiner stands two feet behind the patient and occludes the ear not being tested, then whispers a three-item sequence twice.
Stand two feet in front of the patient so they can see your mouth
Seeing the mouth is exactly what the test has to prevent, which is why the examiner stands behind.
Stand across the room and speak at conversational volume
The test is a quiet whisper at two feet; conversational volume tests nothing.

A.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
A.q: How should psychological stress be regarded in a patient with a skin disorder?
opts: It is the single commonest cause of chronic skin disease
Stress is seldom the sole cause of skin disease, although it can exacerbate many dermatoses.
It has no demonstrable effect on the course of skin disease
Stress does affect skin disease: it is seldom the sole cause, but it can exacerbate many dermatoses.
It should be raised only after organic causes have been excluded
Psychosocial factors are part of the routine history rather than a diagnosis of exclusion.
It is seldom the sole cause, but it can exacerbate many dermatoses
Correct — the distinction between causing and worsening is the point being made.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Besides the whispered voice, which two bedside hearing screens are used?
opts: Weber and Rinne
Weber and Rinne are tuning fork tests that distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss; they are not bedside screens.
Finger rub and a watch
Correct — both are crude but immediately available, and both test whether any sound is heard at all.
Tuning fork and audiometry
The tuning fork tests distinguish the TYPE of loss; they are not screens for its presence, and audiometry is not a bedside screen.
Otoscopy and insufflation
Both examine the ear structurally rather than screening hearing.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Submandibular swelling and erythema with cellulitis of the floor of the mouth. Which description fits?
opts: A peritonsillar abscess — the danger is rupture
A peritonsillar abscess deviates one tonsil; it is not a floor-of-mouth cellulitis.
A submandibular stone — the danger is infection
A stone causes obstruction and swelling at meals, not spreading cellulitis.
Ludwig's angina — it is life threatening because of the AIRWAY
Correct. The swelling pushes the tongue and floor of mouth upward and back, and the airway is the reason this cannot wait.
Ludwig's angina — the danger is spread to the mediastinum only
Ludwig's angina is right, but its life-threatening danger is the airway, not spread to the mediastinum.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which chain comes FIRST in the standard sequence for palpating the neck nodes?
opts: Preauricular

Correct. The sequence runs preauricular, postauricular, occipital, tonsillar, submandibular, submental, superficial cervical, posterior cervical, deep cervical, supraclavicular — following a route so none is missed.
Supraclavicular
Supraclavicular nodes come last in the sequence, which begins at the preauricular nodes.
Submental
Submental nodes come after the submandibular nodes, well after the preauricular nodes that start the sequence.
Deep cervical
Deep cervical nodes come near the end, just before supraclavicular; the sequence starts preauricular.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which two conditions are associated with blepharitis?
opts: Graves disease and myasthenia gravis
Graves disease causes proptosis and myasthenia gravis causes ptosis; blepharitis goes with bacteria and atopic dermatitis.
Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus
Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus go with nodular episcleritis; blepharitis goes with bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis.
Bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis
Correct — blepharitis is a common eye inflammation associated with bacterial infections and with atopic dermatitis.
Hypothyroidism and iron deficiency
Hypothyroidism shows as lateral eyebrow sparseness; blepharitis is associated with bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 31

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: In a trauma patient, what must NOT be done?
opts: Do not measure visual acuity
Visual acuity is still tested in trauma, following the same pattern as a routine eye examination; the globe is not palpated.
Do not inspect the lids
The eyelids are still examined in trauma as part of the routine pattern; what must not be done is palpating the globe.
Do not take a history
The history still matters, including tetanus status and any chemical's acidity; what must not be done is palpating the globe.
Do not palpate the globe
Correct — in trauma it is critical not to palpate the globe, and too much pressure on a ruptured globe is a known mistake.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 24

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Watery or mucoid discharge suggests which conditions?
opts: Acute iritis
Acute iritis produces no ocular discharge; watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergic or viral conditions.
Acute glaucoma
Acute glaucoma produces no ocular discharge; watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergic or viral conditions.
Allergic or viral
Correct — watery or mucoid discharge goes with allergic or viral conditions, while purulent discharge suggests bacteria.
Bacterial infection
Bacterial infections produce purulent discharge; watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergic or viral conditions.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 19

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What is the Centor rule used for?
opts: Predicting which patients need tonsillectomy
Centor guides testing and treatment for an acute sore throat; the decision about tonsillectomy is a separate, longer-term one.
Deciding, from clinical features, how likely a sore throat is to be bacterial
Correct. It is a clinical prediction rule — it converts findings into a probability and a course of action.
Grading the severity of tonsillar enlargement
Tonsil size is not part of the rule. Centor converts four clinical features into a probability of bacterial infection.
Distinguishing peritonsillar abscess from tonsillitis
Centor does not separate abscess from tonsillitis; it estimates how likely a sore throat is to be streptococcal.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What does reduced mobility of the tympanic membrane on insufflation indicate?
opts: Sensorineural hearing loss
Insufflation assesses the middle ear mechanically and says nothing about the cochlea.
Effusion behind the membrane
Correct. Reduced mobility on insufflation points to an effusion behind the membrane or to a thickened tympanic membrane.
Perforation of the membrane
A perforation prevents a pressure change being held at all, so the test cannot be interpreted that way.
Cerumen impaction in the canal
Cerumen in the canal is seen directly on otoscopy; reduced mobility points to an effusion or a thickened membrane.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: A brown to black discoloration of the nail should raise concern for which diagnosis?
opts: Melanoma
Correct — pigmented change in a nail warrants the same concern as a pigmented skin lesion.
Pseudomonas infection
Pseudomonas infection turns the nail green; a brown to black nail should raise concern for melanoma.
Iron deficiency
That is associated with koilonychia rather than pigment change.
Psoriasis
Psoriasis produces pitting and onycholysis rather than brown-black pigment.

A.io: g — Documentation of a complete history and physical examination
A.q: How should physical examination findings be recorded in a written clinical note?
opts: Assign each system a numeric score on a standard scale
Numeric scores are not used; findings are described in words instead of being labeled normal, abnormal or unremarkable.
Describe what was found, rather than writing normal, abnormal or unremarkable
Correct — a description communicates what was actually observed, where a label does not.
Use unremarkable wherever nothing is wrong, to keep the note concise
Unremarkable is one of the labels to avoid; findings are described in words instead of being written as normal, abnormal or unremarkable.
Record only the abnormal findings and omit the normal ones entirely
Normal findings are still recorded; every finding is described in words rather than being labeled normal, abnormal or unremarkable.
A.cite: Intro to PD II - Elwaya .pdf, Page 20

A.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
A.q: Which primary lesion usually precedes a crust?
opts: A wheal
A wheal is solid, transient edema; the lesion that usually precedes a crust is a vesicle, bulla or pustule.
A nodule or tumor
Nodules and tumors are solid masses; the usual antecedents of a crust are a vesicle, bulla or pustule.
A vesicle, bulla or pustule
Correct — each of the three ruptures and leaves dried serum, blood and debris behind.
A macule or patch
A macule or patch is a flat discoloration; a crust usually follows a vesicle, bulla or pustule.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Purulent discharge suggests what?
opts: Bacterial infection
Correct — purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection, while watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergy or a virus.
Allergic conjunctivitis
Allergic conditions give watery or mucoid discharge; purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection.
Viral conjunctivitis
Viral conditions give watery or mucoid discharge; purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection.
Dry eye
Dryness points to lacrimal obstruction or Sjogren's syndrome; purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 19

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Gradual, painless visual loss suggests what?
opts: Simple glaucoma or cataract
Correct — gradual, painless visual loss suggests simple glaucoma or cataracts.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Acute narrow angle glaucoma is acute and painful; gradual, painless loss suggests simple glaucoma or cataract.
Vitreous hemorrhage
Vitreous hemorrhage is an acute, unilateral, painless cause; gradual painless loss suggests simple glaucoma or cataract.
Chemical exposure
Chemical exposure is acute, bilateral and painful; gradual painless loss suggests simple glaucoma or cataract.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 16

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: How do you assess whether the eyes are truly protruding?
opts: Stand behind the seated patient and inspect from above
Correct — stand behind the seated patient, look down from above, and draw the lids up to compare the corneas with the lower lids.
Sit facing the patient and compare the two eyes directly
Prominent eyes are judged from behind and above the seated patient, comparing the corneas with the lower lids.
Shine a light from the temporal side and look for a shadow
Oblique light from the temporal side looks for the iris shadow of a narrow angle; protrusion is judged from behind and above.
Palpate the globe to judge its forward position
The globe is not palpated, and it is critical not to in trauma; protrusion is judged by inspecting from behind and above.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 25

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: How is the auricle positioned to straighten the ear canal for otoscopy in an adult?
opts: Leave it undisturbed and advance the speculum slowly
Without straightening the canal the speculum meets the canal wall, which is both painful and uninformative.
Pull it up, back, and away from the head
Correct — all three directions. The canal is not straight, and the view is only as good as the alignment.
Pull it down and back
That is the maneuver for an infant, whose canal runs differently.
Press it forward against the cheek
Pressing the auricle forward does not straighten the canal; the auricle is pulled up, back and away from the head.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: Which malignancy is the most frequent neoplasm occurring in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome?
opts: Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is common in the general population but is not the neoplasm associated with this condition.
Malignant melanoma
Melanoma is not the neoplasm most frequently associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
Squamous cell carcinoma
This arises on sun-exposed skin and is not the associated neoplasm.
Kaposi's sarcoma
Correct — the lesions start light colored and coalesce into darker blue-purple macules, papules, nodules and plaques.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: How does the RATE of onset of visual impairment guide the differential?
opts: Rate of onset does not narrow the differential
The rate of onset does give a clue to etiology: rapid deterioration suggests vascular causes, gradual loss cataract.
Rapid deterioration always means trauma
Rapid deterioration points to vascular causes, not trauma; gradual loss suggests causes such as cataract.
Rapid deterioration suggests a vascular cause
Correct — rapid deterioration should make you strongly consider vascular causes, while gradual loss suggests causes such as cataract.
Rapid deterioration suggests cataract; gradual loss suggests a vascular cause
This reverses the pairing: rapid deterioration points to vascular causes, and gradual loss to causes such as cataract.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 11

A.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
A.q: Psoriasis characteristically appears in which distribution?
opts: Dermatomal
A dermatomal distribution suggests herpes zoster; psoriasis characteristically involves the extensor surfaces.
Extensor
Correct — the elbows and knees are the classic extensor sites.
Flexor
A flexor distribution is typical of intertrigo; psoriasis characteristically involves the extensor surfaces.
Photodistributed
A sun-exposed distribution suggests skin cancers; psoriasis characteristically involves the extensor surfaces.

A.io: h — Involving the patient in healthcare communication
A.q: When a third party supplies the patient's responses during an assessed encounter, where should your attention stay?
opts: Divided evenly between the patient and the person answering
Attention is not split between them; you should always be looking at and interacting with the patient, not the person answering.
On the patient, interacting with the patient rather than the person supplying the answers
Correct — you should always be looking at and interacting with the patient, even when the responses are supplied by someone else.
On whoever is supplying the answers, since that is the source of information
The person supplying the answers is not the patient; you should always be looking at and interacting with the patient instead.
On the documentation form, so that responses are recorded accurately
The documentation form is not the focus; you should always be looking at and interacting with the patient throughout the encounter.
A.cite: Intro to PD II - Elwaya .pdf, Page 8

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: In the melanoma warning signs, what does D stand for?
opts: Darkening of the surrounding skin
Color variation within the lesion is what the letter C covers.
Diameter larger than six millimeters
Correct — six millimeters is roughly the diameter of a pencil eraser.
Depth of invasion into the dermis
Depth of invasion is not one of the warning signs; D stands for a diameter larger than six millimeters.
Duration of more than six months
The letters describe appearance, not how long the lesion has been present.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: What is nystagmus?
opts: Fine rhythmic oscillation of the eyes
Correct — nystagmus is fine rhythmic oscillation of the eyes, and a few beats on lateral gaze are normal.
Misalignment of the visual axes — a few degrees is normal
Nonalignment of the eyes is strabismus; nystagmus is fine rhythmic oscillation of the eyes.
Drooping of the upper lid — a few millimeters is normal
Drooping of the upper lid is ptosis; nystagmus is fine rhythmic oscillation of the eyes.
Unequal pupil size — a few millimeters is normal
Unequal pupils are anisocoria, where half to one millimeter is common; nystagmus is fine rhythmic oscillation of the eyes.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 63

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Why might a patient with conductive hearing loss say they hear BETTER in a noisy room?
opts: The patient compensates by lip reading, which is easier in company
Lip reading may help in company, but the effect here is acoustic rather than behavioral.
The conductive block attenuates the background noise along with everything else
Correct. Others raise their voices over the noise while the patient's block filters the noise itself, so the speech-to-noise ratio improves.
Noise stimulates the cochlear hair cells directly
There is no such effect, and in conductive loss the cochlea was never the problem.
Conductive loss spares the high frequencies that carry noise
Conductive loss has little effect on which sounds are lost; it is the sensorineural pattern that takes the high registers.

A.io: a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
A.q: Which glands become active during puberty and secrete pheromones?
opts: Apocrine glands
Correct. Their activation at puberty is what distinguishes them from eccrine glands.
Eccrine glands
Eccrine glands are functional from birth and secrete thermoregulatory sweat.
Sebaceous glands
Sebaceous glands surround hair follicles and secrete sebum to keep hair and skin moist; they do not secrete pheromones.
Meibomian glands
These are the modified glands of the eyelid margin and are not the pheromone-secreting glands.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Nasal polyps are associated with which conditions?
opts: Asthma, aspirin sensitivity and cystic fibrosis
Correct. Nasal polyps are associated with allergic rhinitis, aspirin sensitivity, asthma, chronic sinus infection and cystic fibrosis.
Hypertension, anticoagulation and atherosclerosis
Hypertension, anticoagulation and atherosclerosis are not polyp associations; polyps go with asthma, allergy and cystic fibrosis.
Smoking, alcohol and reflux
Smoking, alcohol and reflux relate to hoarseness and tobacco history; polyps go with asthma and aspirin sensitivity.
Diabetes, obesity and sleep apnea
Diabetes, obesity and sleep apnea are not polyp associations; polyps go with allergy, aspirin sensitivity, asthma and cystic fibrosis.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which part of the hand is used to palpate the lymph nodes of the neck?
opts: The fingertips of all four fingers
Four fingertips are not the technique; neck nodes are palpated with the pads of the index and middle fingers.
The thumb and index finger in a pincer grip
A pincer grip is not used; the pads of the index and middle fingers palpate each chain of neck nodes.
The ulnar border of the hand
That is the otoscopy anchoring point, not a palpation surface.
The pads of the index and middle fingers
Correct. The pads are the most sensitive surface, and two fingers cover a node without rolling past it.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which two structures are commonly left unexamined?
opts: The eyelids and eyebrows
Lids and brows are not among the common omissions; the structures commonly missed are the cornea and lens.
The lacrimal sac and puncta
The lacrimal sac is not among the common omissions; the structures commonly missed are the cornea and lens.
The extraocular muscles
Eye movements are not among the common omissions; the two structures commonly missed are the cornea and lens.
The cornea and the lens
Correct — failure to examine the cornea and lens is one of the common mistakes in the eye examination.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 20

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: Alopecia areata is associated with which category of disease?
opts: Psychiatric disorders
Trichotillomania is the hair loss driven by an urge to pull.
Endocrine disorders of androgen excess
Androgen excess is not the association; alopecia areata is a chronic inflammatory follicle disease linked to autoimmune disorders.
Autoimmune disorders
Correct — it is a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicles.
Fungal infections
Fungal infection of the scalp is tinea capitis, a separate diagnosis.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: What does the term hirsutism describe?
opts: Increased hair growth in women following a male pattern of distribution
Correct — the pattern of distribution, not simply the amount, defines the term.
Diffuse thinning of hair in women after menopause
Thinning after menopause is a form of alopecia; hirsutism is increased hair growth in women in a male pattern.
Loss of hair in multiple round patches
Hair loss in multiple round patches is alopecia areata; hirsutism is increased hair growth in women in a male pattern.
Excessive fine hair covering the whole body in infancy
Hirsutism is not an infant finding; it is increased hair growth in women following a male pattern of distribution.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which of these belongs in the URGENT group, seen by ophthalmology within a day or less?
opts: Dry eye and blepharitis
Neither is on the urgent list, which includes acute glaucoma, orbital cellulitis, retinal detachment and hyphema.
Pinguecula and pterygium
A pinguecula is harmless, and neither is on the urgent list, which includes acute glaucoma and retinal detachment.
Acute glaucoma
Correct — acute glaucoma is on the urgent list with orbital cellulitis, corneal ulcer or abrasion, retinal detachment and hyphema.
Sudden vision loss, chemical burns and globe rupture
Those are emergent complaints, referred to ophthalmology immediately rather than within a day.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 124

A.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
A.q: Which processes can convert a primary lesion into a secondary one?
opts: Only the passage of time, independent of any external factor
Time alone is not the cause; the change comes from disease progression, treatment, or manipulation such as picking or scratching.
Only secondary bacterial infection of the original lesion
Infection is not one of the three; the causes are disease progression, treatment, and manipulation such as picking or scratching.
Disease progression, treatment, and manipulation such as picking or scratching
Correct — the patient's own handling of a lesion is as capable of changing it as the disease itself.
Disease progression alone, since treatment does not alter lesion morphology
Treatment is one of the causes; disease progression, treatment and manipulation such as picking or scratching all change a lesion.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What does UNILATERAL nasal obstruction suggest?
opts: Allergic rhinitis
Allergic rhinitis affects the nose as a whole rather than one side.
Viral rhinitis
Viral rhinitis congests both sides. Unilateral obstruction is what points to a structural cause.
Rhinitis medicamentosa
Rhinitis medicamentosa belongs to the medication history; unilateral obstruction points to a foreign body, tumor or deviated septum.
A foreign body
Correct. Unilateral obstruction suggests a foreign body, a tumor or a deviated septum, all structural causes on the blocked side.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: A purple lesion does not fade when a glass slide is pressed against it. What does this indicate?
opts: Inadequate peripheral circulation
Cyanosis from poor circulation is not what the maneuver assesses.
Hemorrhage in the skin
Correct — blood outside the vessels cannot be displaced by pressure, which is why petechiae and purpura do not blanch.
Vascular engorgement
Engorged vessels empty under pressure so the color fades; color that does not fade means hemorrhage in the skin.
An allergic reaction
Diascopy distinguishes hemorrhage from engorgement rather than identifying allergy.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: You lift a fold of skin and release it, and the skin remains elevated. What does this indicate?
opts: Lichenification
Lichenification is thickening with accentuated skin lines from chronic irritation.
Scleroderma
This condition is not among those assessed by the turgor maneuver here.
Dehydration
Correct. Normal skin resumes its shape quickly; skin that stays tented has lost turgor.
Edema
Edema reduces mobility, meaning the skin will not lift easily in the first place.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Cracking and inflammation at the CORNERS of the mouth. What is this called?
opts: Angioedema
Angioedema is a separate lip abnormality; red, cracked sores at the corners of the mouth are angular cheilitis.
Herpes simplex
Herpes gives grouped vesicles, typically at the vermilion border rather than the angles.
Aphthous ulceration
Aphthous ulcers are painful round sores inside the mouth, not cracking at the corners, which is angular cheilitis.
Angular cheilitis
Correct — one of three lip abnormalities to recognize, alongside angioedema and herpes simplex.

A.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
A.q: A linear crack in the skin, as seen in athlete's foot, is called what?
opts: A fissure
Correct — the interdigital spaces of the foot are the classic site.
An erosion
An erosion is a broader loss of superficial epidermis with a moist surface; a linear crack in the skin is a fissure.
An excoriation
An excoriation is a scratch mark and may be linear or rounded.
A scale
A scale is a thin flake of exfoliated epidermis; a linear crack, as in athlete's foot, is a fissure.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Bilateral visual loss usually implies which kind of problem?
opts: A primary neurologic cause rather than a primary ophthalmologic one
Correct — bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology and not a primary ophthalmologic problem.
A primary ophthalmologic cause
It runs the other way: bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology, not an ophthalmologic one.
An infective cause
Infection is not the usual inference; bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology.
A traumatic cause
Trauma is not the usual inference; bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology rather than an eye problem.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 10 (speaker notes)

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: A sore AND SMOOTH tongue suggests what?
opts: Geographic tongue
Geographic tongue is a benign pattern of map-like patches, and it is not smooth.
Oral candidiasis
Candidal infection gives plaques rather than a smooth surface.
Nutritional deficiency
Correct. The smoothness is loss of papillae, and that combination of sore and smooth is the pointer.
Aphthous ulceration
Aphthous ulcers are discrete painful lesions, not diffuse smoothing.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: Firm stroking of a patient's skin produces a red line, a broadening flare, and then a linear wheal. What is this called?
opts: The triple response of Lewis
Correct — capillary dilatation, arteriolar dilatation and then transudation of fluid, in that sequence.
The diascopy response
Diascopy involves pressing glass against the skin rather than stroking it.
An excoriation
An excoriation is an abrasion or scratch mark; firm stroking that gives a red line, flare and wheal is the triple response of Lewis.
Lichenification
Lichenification is thickening with accentuated skin lines from chronic irritation, not a red line, flare and wheal after one stroke.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: Which hair characteristics are assessed by inspection rather than palpation?
opts: All four characteristics by inspection alone
Not all four are seen; texture is assessed by palpation, while color, distribution and quantity are inspected.
All four characteristics by palpation alone
Not all four are felt; color, distribution and quantity are assessed by inspection, and only texture by palpation.
Color, distribution and quantity by inspection
Correct — color, distribution and quantity are inspected, leaving texture as the one hair characteristic assessed by palpation.
Texture by inspection; color and quantity by palpation
The assignments are reversed: texture is palpated, while color, distribution and quantity are inspected.

A.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
A.q: You see a patient whose skin, hair and nail hygiene appears inadequate. What should this prompt you to assess?
opts: The social history
Correct. Patients with cognitive problems may not attend to hygiene measures, so poor hygiene is a clinical finding worth explaining. Cognition and ability to perform activities of daily living.
Whether the patient is being truthful about how often they bathe
The purpose is to identify a barrier to self-care rather than to challenge the patient.
Nutritional status through serum albumin and prealbumin levels
Laboratory assessment is not what inadequate hygiene should prompt.
Whether the patient has access to running water at home
Running water is not the focus; poor hygiene prompts assessment of social history, cognition and ability to perform activities of daily living.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Which statement correctly defines OD and OU?
opts: OD is the left eye; OS is the right
This swaps them: OD is the right eye and OS the left eye, while OU refers to both eyes.
OD is the right eye; OU is both eyes
Correct — OD refers to the right eye, OS to the left eye and OU to both eyes.
OS is the right eye; OD is both eyes
OS refers to the left eye, and OD is the right eye; both eyes are recorded as OU.
OU is the right eye; OS is both eyes
OU refers to both eyes and OS to the left eye; the right eye is recorded as OD.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 49

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: What is microtia?
opts: An abnormally small auricle
Correct. Microtia is a congenitally underdeveloped, abnormally small auricle, and it is grouped with atresia among the congenital deformities.
An absent or closed ear canal
That is atresia, which often accompanies microtia but is a separate finding.
An extra accessory auricle
An extra accessory auricle is a supernumerary auricle, a separate congenital deformity; microtia is an abnormally small auricle.
A small pit anterior to the tragus
A small pit in front of the ear is a preauricular sinus or pit; microtia is an abnormally small auricle.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Acute, unilateral and PAINFUL visual loss usually localizes to where?
opts: Usually the cornea and anterior chamber
Correct — acute, unilateral, painful causes usually sit in the cornea and anterior chamber: abrasion or ulcer, uveitis, hyphema, angle closure.
Usually the retina — vascular occlusion and detachment
Retinal vascular occlusion and detachment are acute, unilateral PAINLESS causes; the painful ones sit in the cornea and anterior chamber.
Usually the optic nerve — optic neuritis alone
Optic neuritis is not the grouping; acute, unilateral, painful causes usually sit in the cornea and anterior chamber.
Usually the lids — blepharitis and hordeolum
Lid conditions are not in this group; acute, unilateral, painful causes usually sit in the cornea and anterior chamber.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 16

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Why should dentures be removed during the oral examination?
opts: To let the patient speak more clearly during the history
Speech is not the reason; dentures are removed so the mucosa beneath them can be inspected for ulcers and lesions.
To look underneath for ulcers and lesions
Correct. A denture hides exactly the mucosa most at risk from chronic irritation.
To assess the fit of the denture itself
Denture fit is not the reason; dentures come out so the mucosa beneath them can be checked for ulcers and lesions.
To allow the tongue blade to be inserted
The tongue blade is for seeing the posterior pharynx; the dentures come out so the mucosa beneath them can be inspected.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Which immunization status matters in eye trauma?
opts: Pneumococcal
Pneumococcal status is not the one tied to eye trauma; tetanus immunization status is what matters after an eye injury.
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis B status is not the one tied to eye trauma; tetanus immunization status is what matters after an eye injury.
Tetanus
Correct — tetanus immunization status is important in any patient with a history of eye trauma.
Influenza
Influenza status is not the one tied to eye trauma; tetanus immunization status is what matters after an eye injury.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 15

B.io: a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
B.q: Which gland surrounds the hair follicle and keeps hair and skin moist?
opts: The eccrine gland
Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface and secrete sweat for temperature control.
The apocrine gland
Apocrine glands secrete pheromones and switch on at puberty.
The sudoriferous gland
Sudoriferous is the other name for the eccrine gland, which secretes sweat to maintain body temperature rather than sebum.
The sebaceous gland
Correct — sebaceous glands surround the hair follicles and secrete sebum, which keeps hair and skin moist.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Which features mark vertigo as CENTRAL rather than peripheral?
opts: Aural fullness with fluctuating tinnitus
Ear fullness with fluctuating tinnitus is Ménière disease, a peripheral cause in which hearing is also affected.
Brainstem deficits such as dysarthria and ataxia
Correct. Central vertigo usually comes with other brainstem deficits (dysarthria, ataxia, crossed motor and sensory deficits), while hearing is unaffected and tinnitus absent.
Hearing impaired on one side with tinnitus present
That combination points peripheral — acoustic neuroma in particular.
Episodes lasting under a minute triggered by head position
Brief episodes set off by rolling over or tilting the head describe benign positional vertigo, a peripheral cause.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Which compensatory finding accompanies diplopia?
opts: A compensatory squint of one eye only
A squint is itself improper alignment of the eyes, a cause of diplopia; the compensation is a head posture.
Compensatory pupil dilation
Pupil dilation is not a compensation for double vision; the accompanying finding is a compensatory head posture.
Compensatory tearing
Tearing points to lacrimal obstruction or Sjogren's syndrome; diplopia is accompanied by a compensatory head posture.
A compensatory head posture
Correct — diplopia can be accompanied by a compensatory head posture, alongside faulty alignment of the eyes.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 18

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What does an acuity of 20/200 mean?
opts: The patient has 200 degrees of visual field at 20 feet
Snellen notation measures acuity, not the field; at 20 feet the patient reads print normal vision reads at 200 feet.
At 20 feet the patient reads print that a person with normal vision could read at 200 feet
Correct — at 20 feet the patient reads what normal vision reads at 200 feet; the larger the second number, the worse the vision.
At 200 feet the patient reads print that a normal eye reads at 20 feet
This reverses the distances: the patient stands at 20 feet, and 200 feet is where normal vision reads the same print.
The patient sees 20 percent of normal at 200 feet
The notation is not a percentage; at 20 feet the patient reads print that normal vision reads at 200 feet.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 49

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Which description of exostoses is correct?
opts: Benign bony growths in the ear canal, causing conductive loss
Correct. They narrow the canal mechanically, which is why the loss is conductive.
Benign bony growths on the ossicles, causing sensorineural loss
They are canal growths, and any canal problem produces conductive loss.
Malignant bone tumors of the temporal bone
Exostoses are benign bony growths in the canal; a malignant temporal bone tumor is a different problem entirely.
Cholesterol deposits in the middle ear
Exostoses are not middle-ear deposits of any kind. They are benign bony growths, and they sit in the canal.

B.io: c — Clinical reasoning in oral presentations
B.q: Which findings belong in an oral case presentation?
opts: Only the abnormal findings, since normal findings add nothing
Pertinent negatives carry as much weight as positives in narrowing a differential.
Only the physical examination findings, since the history is documented separately
Both the history and the examination contribute to the presentation.
Pertinent positives and negatives from both the history and the physical examination
Correct. Choosing what counts as pertinent is the clinical reasoning being assessed.
Every finding obtained, whether positive or negative
A presentation is a selected vignette rather than a complete transcript of the encounter.
B.cite: Intro to PD II - Elwaya .pdf, Page 9

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: How is the tongue palpated?
opts: Palpate with both hands simultaneously from below the jaw
That is bimanual palpation of the floor of the mouth, a separate maneuver.
Ask the patient to protrude the tongue and palpate the tip only
Palpating only the tip misses the lateral border and undersurface, where tongue cancers usually appear.
Use a tongue blade to depress and palpate through it
The blade is used to see the posterior pharynx, not to palpate the tongue.
Hold it with gauze in one hand and palpate with the other
Correct. Holding the tongue with gauze in the right hand, palpate with the left, then switch hands to reach the other side.

B.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
B.q: What distinguishes a primary skin lesion from a secondary one?
opts: A primary lesion is the one the patient noticed first
The distinction is about the disease process, not about what the patient happened to notice.
A primary lesion forms first and results directly from the disease
Correct — a primary lesion forms first and results directly from the disease; a secondary lesion is a change in it over time.
A primary lesion is larger than one centimeter and a secondary lesion is smaller
Size distinguishes several individual lesions from one another but not the two categories.
A primary lesion is flat and a secondary lesion is elevated
Flatness does not separate them; a primary lesion forms first from the disease, and a secondary lesion is its change over time.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Dome-shaped, bright red to violet or black lesions also known as Campbell De Morgan spots are called what?
opts: Spider angiomas
Spider angiomas have radiating arms from a central red macule; dome-shaped red to violet lesions are cherry angiomas.
Telangiectasias
Telangiectasias are fine, irregular blanching vessels; dome-shaped red to violet lesions are cherry angiomas.
Ecchymoses
An ecchymosis is a flat purple macule that fades over time; dome-shaped red to black lesions are cherry angiomas.
Cherry angiomas
Correct — cherry angiomas are dome shaped, bright red to violet or black, and may or may not blanch.

B.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
B.q: Which historical factors should be explored for their relationship to the appearance of skin lesions?
opts: The patient's blood type and immunization record
Blood type and immunizations are not explored; the factors are season, travel, heat or cold, previous reactions, drugs and menses.
Season, travel, heat or cold, previous reactions, drugs and menses
Correct — each can be the trigger that explains the timing of an eruption.
Season and travel only, since the remainder are rarely relevant
Season and travel are only two; heat or cold, previous reactions, drugs and menses are also explored in relation to the lesions.
The patient's height, weight and body mass index
These are not among the relationships explored in a skin history.

B.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
B.q: What distinguishes a bulla from a vesicle?
opts: A bulla contains purulent material and a vesicle contains clear fluid
Purulent content defines a pustule; a bulla and a vesicle both contain fluid and differ only in size.
A bulla is deeper in the dermis than a vesicle
Both are superficial elevations; a bulla differs from a vesicle only by being larger than one centimeter.
A bulla is solid and a vesicle is fluid-filled
Both are filled with fluid; a bulla is larger than one centimeter and a vesicle is smaller.
A bulla is larger than one centimeter and a vesicle is smaller
Correct — both are superficial elevations filled with fluid, and only size separates them.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: A patient reports ear pain but the ear itself looks entirely normal. Which structures should the history now cover?
opts: The thyroid gland and the trachea
Both belong to the neck examination; referred ear pain comes from the jaw joint, the teeth and the cervical spine.
The parotid and submandibular salivary glands
The salivary glands are not among the referred sources. The cranial nerves that carry the referral are V, VII, IX and X.
The jaw joint, the teeth and the cervical spine
Correct. Ear pain is frequently referred, and these three are the usual sources — the first answer a patient gives is not the last question you ask.
The frontal and maxillary sinuses
Sinus tenderness is part of the nose examination. Referred otalgia comes from the joint, the teeth and the cervical spine.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Which of these complaints should be referred to ophthalmology IMMEDIATELY?
opts: Corneal abrasion
A corneal abrasion is urgent, not emergent: it needs ophthalmology follow-up within one day or less.
Chemical burn
Correct — chemical burns are emergent and go to ophthalmology immediately, as do rupture and sudden vision loss.
Hyphema
Hyphema is urgent, not emergent: it needs ophthalmology follow-up within one day or less.
Orbital cellulitis
Orbital cellulitis is urgent, not emergent: it needs ophthalmology follow-up within one day or less.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 124

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is chemosis?
opts: Forward displacement of the eye in the orbit
That is proptosis, forward displacement of the eye; chemosis is swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva.
Outward turning of the lower eyelid
That is ectropion, outward turning of the lower lid; chemosis is swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva.
Swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva
Correct — chemosis is swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva itself, not of the lids or the globe.
Injection of the superficially visible vessels of the conjunctiva or sclera
That is hyperemia, injection of the superficially visible vessels; chemosis is swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 3

B.io: c — Clinical reasoning in oral presentations
B.q: In what order should an oral case presentation generally proceed?
opts: In reverse, opening with the diagnosis and working back to the evidence
The presentation builds toward the assessment rather than announcing it first.
Grouped by body system in alphabetical order
Alphabetical grouping is not used; a presentation mostly follows the order in which the history was obtained and the examination performed.
Physical examination findings first, then the history that prompted them
Leading with the examination reverses the encounter; the history comes first because a presentation follows the order the encounter ran.
Mostly the order in which the history was obtained and the examination performed
Correct. Following the encounter's own sequence is what makes it easy to follow.
B.cite: Intro to PD II - Elwaya .pdf, Page 9

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: A non-blanching reddish-purple macule measuring six millimeters is called what?
opts: Purpura
Correct — the three millimeter to one centimeter range defines purpura.
A petechia
A petechia is smaller than three millimeters; a six-millimeter non-blanching macule is purpura.
An ecchymosis
An ecchymosis exceeds one centimeter; six millimeters falls in purpura's range of three millimeters to one centimeter.
A telangiectasia
A telangiectasia is a fine irregular vessel that blanches; a non-blanching six-millimeter macule is purpura.

B.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
B.q: You lift a fold of skin and it does not lift with ease. What does reduced skin mobility suggest?
opts: Recent sun exposure
Sun exposure does not tether the skin; normal skin lifts up with ease, and reduced mobility points to edema.
Edema
Correct — fluid within the tissue tethers the skin and reduces how freely it moves.
Dehydration
Dehydration is detected by turgor, where the skin remains elevated after being released.
Normal aging of the skin
Aging is not the explanation; normal skin lifts up with ease, and skin that will not lift has reduced mobility from edema.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Small depressions in the nail plate representing dystrophy of the plate are called what?
opts: Nail pitting
Correct — the pits are areas of small depressions in the nail plate.
Splinter hemorrhages
Splinter hemorrhages are hemorrhages of the distal capillary loop.
Beau's lines
Beau's lines are transverse depressions running across the nail.
Koilonychia
Koilonychia is a spoon-shaped concave nail; small depressions from nail plate dystrophy are nail pitting.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is the underlying lesion in Adie's tonic pupil?
opts: Degeneration of the ciliary ganglia and the postganglionic parasympathetic fibers
Correct — Adie's pupil results from degeneration of the ciliary ganglia and the postganglionic parasympathetic fibers.
Interruption of the sympathetic supply
Interrupted sympathetic supply produces Horner syndrome's small pupil; Adie's comes from ciliary ganglion degeneration.
Compression of the oculomotor nerve
Oculomotor compression gives a dilated pupil fixed to light and near; Adie's comes from ciliary ganglion degeneration.
Demyelination of the optic nerve
Optic nerve disease causes an afferent defect; Adie's comes from degeneration of the ciliary ganglia and parasympathetic fibers.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 82

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Which finding defines a stage IV pressure ulcer?
opts: Non-blanching erythema over intact skin
Non-blanching erythema over intact skin is stage I; stage IV destroys tissue, muscle and bone.
Full thickness skin loss with destruction of tissue, muscle and bone
Correct — involvement of muscle and bone is what separates stage IV from stage III.
Full thickness skin loss reaching but not penetrating muscle
Full thickness loss reaching but not through muscle is stage III; stage IV destroys tissue, muscle and bone.
Partial thickness loss of the epidermis and dermis
Partial thickness loss is stage II; stage IV is full thickness loss that destroys tissue, muscle and bone.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Which speculum size should be used for pneumatic otoscopy?
opts: A medium speculum regardless of canal size
A fixed medium size ignores the canal; the speculum must be the largest that will fit, so that it forms a proper seal.
Whichever gives the widest field of view, seal notwithstanding
Field of view is not the constraint — the seal is what the insufflation depends on.
The largest that will fit the canal
Correct. Insufflation needs a proper seal in the canal, so the largest speculum that will fit the canal is the one to use.
The smallest available, to reduce discomfort
Comfort is not the criterion, and a small speculum cannot seal the canal.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Why does the ABSENCE of cough count toward the Centor score rather than its presence?
opts: A cough points toward a viral cause
Correct. A cough points toward a viral cause, so its absence raises the probability of streptococcal pharyngitis and scores a point.
Coughing masks tonsillar exudates on examination
Cough does not hide exudates, which score as their own criterion; the rule separates streptococcal from viral sore throat.
A cough indicates the infection has spread to the lower airway
The criterion is about separating bacterial from viral pharyngitis, not about tracking spread to the lower airway.
Cough is a criterion only in children
Absence of cough scores for any patient; age enters the modified score separately, not through cough.

B.io: e — Comprehensive versus focused history and examination
B.q: What distinguishes a focused encounter from a comprehensive one?
opts: The history and examination are both narrowed to what the presenting problem requires
Correct — a focused encounter is not a shorter version of everything, it is a targeted selection.
The examination is narrowed but the history remains complete
The history is not kept complete; in a focused encounter both the history and the physical examination are narrowed to the problem.
The history is narrowed but every system is still examined
Every system is not examined; in a focused encounter the physical examination is narrowed as well as the history.
The encounter is identical but documented more briefly
The difference is in what is gathered, not only in how it is written up.
B.cite: Intro to PD II - Elwaya .pdf, Page 7

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: In unilateral CONDUCTIVE loss, which way does the Weber sound lateralize?
opts: It does not lateralize in conductive loss
Lateralization is precisely what the test detects, and conductive loss produces it.
It alternates between ears
Alternating lateralization is not a recognized Weber result; the sound goes one way or stays midline.
To the IMPAIRED ear
Correct. Sound lateralizes to the impaired ear, because room noise is not well heard on that side, so detection of the vibrations improves.
To the GOOD ear, because the impaired ear transmits nothing
That is the sensorineural pattern. In conductive loss the cochlea is intact and hears the bone-conducted tone perfectly.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: A MULTINODULAR enlarged thyroid carries a risk of malignancy under what circumstance?
opts: When there is a family history
Correct — the multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process, and family history is what raises the concern.
Always, regardless of history
A multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process; it is a family history that raises the concern about malignancy.
Only if the gland is tender
Tenderness points to thyroiditis; a multinodular gland raises malignancy risk when there is a family history.
Only in patients under thirty
Age is not the qualifier; a multinodular enlarged thyroid raises malignancy risk when there is a family history.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is the normal appearance of the fundus and disc?
opts: White with absent tiny disc vessels
A white disc with absent tiny vessels is optic atrophy, from death of optic nerve fibers.
An enlarged cup with vessels sinking in around the disc
An enlarged cup with vessels sinking in is glaucomatous cupping; the normal cup is less than half the disc diameter.
Yellowish-orange to cream color, small disc vessels, a sharp disc margin, and a cup located centrally or slightly temporal with a diameter normally less than half the disc
Correct — the normal fundus is yellowish orange to cream, with a sharp disc margin and a central cup under half the disc diameter.
Pink with blurred margins and no visible cup
A pink swollen disc with blurred margins and no visible cup is papilledema from raised intracranial pressure.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 102

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is the warning about pressure on a globe that may be ruptured?
opts: Pressure should be applied only with a cotton swab
No instrument makes it safe; too much pressure on a ruptured globe is a recognized mistake, and the globe is not palpated in trauma.
Placing too much pressure on it is a mistake
Correct — failing to diagnose a ruptured globe and placing too much pressure on it are both common examination mistakes.
Pressure is required to assess the depth of injury
Pressure is not used to judge depth; placing too much pressure on a ruptured globe is itself a recognized examination mistake.
Pressure is harmless once an anesthetic is instilled
Anesthetic does not make it safe; placing too much pressure on a ruptured globe is a recognized examination mistake.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 20

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is the pupil finding in an oculomotor nerve palsy?
opts: A small pupil that reacts briskly, with ptosis and anhidrosis
A small, briskly reactive pupil with ptosis and anhidrosis is Horner syndrome, not an oculomotor palsy.
A large pupil with a slow but present near reaction
A large pupil with a very slow but present near reaction is Adie's tonic pupil; the third nerve pupil is fixed.
Small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react
Small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react are Argyll Robertson pupils; the third nerve pupil is dilated and fixed.
A dilated pupil fixed to both light and near effort
Correct — in oculomotor paralysis the dilated pupil is fixed to light and near effort, with ptosis and lateral deviation.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 89

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: How do multiple NEW flashes or floaters differ in significance from a single floater?
opts: Both are always benign
Only the single floater is probably benign; multiple new flashes or floaters could represent a retinal tear or vitreous hemorrhage.
Both always require emergency referral
A single floater is probably benign; it is multiple new flashes or floaters that suggest a retinal tear or vitreous hemorrhage.
Multiple new flashes or floaters suggest a retinal tear or vitreous hemorrhage
Correct — multiple new flashes or floaters could represent a retinal tear or vitreous hemorrhage, while a single floater is probably benign.
A single floater suggests a retinal tear; multiple floaters are benign
This reverses them: a single floater is probably benign, and multiple new flashes or floaters suggest a retinal tear or vitreous hemorrhage.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 10

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: A pressure ulcer shows full thickness skin loss with necrosis of subcutaneous tissue extending down to, but not through, the underlying muscle. What stage is this?
opts: Stage I
In stage I the skin is intact; full thickness loss with necrosis of subcutaneous tissue is stage III.
Stage III
Correct — reaching muscle without destroying it is exactly the stage III boundary.
Stage II
Stage II is partial thickness loss only; full thickness loss with subcutaneous necrosis reaching muscle is stage III.
Stage IV
Stage IV destroys muscle and bone; full thickness loss that reaches but does not go through muscle is stage III.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Vertigo comes on when the patient rolls onto one side in bed, lasts under a minute, and hearing is unaffected. Which is it?
opts: Vestibular neuronitis
Vestibular neuronitis begins suddenly but runs from hours to up to two weeks, not seconds to under a minute.
Acoustic neuroma
Insidious, with impaired hearing on one side and tinnitus present.
Benign positional vertigo
Correct. Sudden onset on rolling onto the affected side or tilting the head up, a few seconds to under a minute, hearing not affected, tinnitus absent.
Ménière disease
Ménière runs several hours to a day or more, and hearing IS affected.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Why does a septal hematoma require URGENT drainage?
opts: To prevent the blood tracking into the orbit
Orbital spread is not the reason; drainage is urgent to prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage.
To prevent airway obstruction
Obstruction may occur but is not why the drainage is urgent.
To prevent secondary sinusitis
Infection is not the reason for urgency; drainage is urgent to prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage.
To prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage
Correct. The cartilage has no blood supply of its own — it depends on the lining that the hematoma has stripped away, so the clock starts immediately.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is the pain of acute iritis like?
opts: Moderate, aching, deep
Correct — acute iritis causes moderate, aching, deep pain, along with decreased vision.
Mild discomfort rather than pain
Mild discomfort rather than pain is conjunctivitis; the pain of acute iritis is moderate, aching and deep.
Severe, aching, deep
Severe, aching, deep pain is glaucoma; the pain of acute iritis is moderate rather than severe.
Absent
Absent pain is subconjunctival hemorrhage; the pain of acute iritis is moderate, aching and deep.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: The Weber test is done and the patient hears the tone only in the LEFT ear. Which ear has sensorineural hearing loss?
opts: The left
That would be true for a conductive loss, which lateralizes TOWARD the affected side.
Neither — this is a normal result
A normal result is midline or heard in both ears; hearing the tone in one ear only means it has lateralized.
Both
Weber evaluates unilateral loss; a bilateral symmetrical loss would not lateralize.
The right
Correct. Sensorineural loss lateralizes AWAY from the damaged side, so hearing the tone on the left places the lesion on the right.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Which description of xanthelasma is accurate?
opts: On the bulbar conjunctiva — consider ultraviolet exposure
A yellowish nodule on the bulbar conjunctiva is a pinguecula; xanthelasma sit nasally on the lids and suggest lipid disorders.
Along the NASAL portions of one or both eyelids — consider lipid disorders
Correct — xanthelasma are raised yellowish plaques along the nasal portions of the eyelids that should prompt a look for lipid disorders.
Along the temporal portions of the lids — consider thyroid disease
The plaques sit on the nasal, not temporal, portions of the lids, and they point to lipid disorders rather than thyroid disease.
At the lid margin — consider bacterial infection
A painful infection at the lid margin is a hordeolum; xanthelasma sit nasally on the lids and suggest lipid disorders.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 34

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Besides non-blanching erythema, which changes characterize a stage I pressure ulcer?
opts: Partial loss of the epidermis with a moist base
Partial thickness skin loss is stage II; stage I keeps the skin intact, with changes in temperature, consistency, sensation and color.
Necrosis extending into subcutaneous tissue
Subcutaneous necrosis is stage III; stage I keeps the skin intact, with changes in temperature, consistency, sensation and color.
Temperature, consistency, sensation and color
Correct — the area may be warm or cool, firm or boggy, and painful or itchy.
Changes in temperature alone
Temperature is only one; consistency, sensation and color also change over the intact skin of a stage I pressure ulcer.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Which of the following is a recognized cause of onycholysis?
opts: Prolonged immersion of the hands in water
Correct — local irritation from chemical exposure or prolonged immersion is one cause, alongside fungal infection, psoriasis, medications such as tetracycline, and trauma.
Iron deficiency producing a thinned nail plate
That mechanism produces koilonychia rather than separation of the plate.
Chronic hypoxia from lung disease
Lung disease is not a cause here; onycholysis follows local irritation, fungal infection, psoriasis, tetracycline or trauma.
A systemic illness three months previously
An illness months earlier leaves Beau's lines; onycholysis follows irritation, fungal infection, psoriasis, tetracycline or trauma.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: What are the four Centor criteria?
opts: Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and ABSENCE of cough
Correct. Three are things present and one is a thing absent, which is the part most often misremembered.
Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and PRESENCE of cough
Cough counts when it is ABSENT — a cough points away from streptococcal infection and toward a viral cause.
Fever, sore throat, headache and myalgia
Sore throat, headache and myalgia are not the criteria; Centor scores fever, exudates, anterior cervical nodes and no cough.
Fever, trismus, uvular deviation and drooling
Those suggest a peritonsillar abscess rather than the scoring rule for pharyngitis.

B.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
B.q: Which skin symptoms should be asked about when taking the history?
opts: Fever, chills and night sweats
These are systemic symptoms covered in the review of systems rather than skin symptoms.
Erythema, scaling and crusting
These are findings you observe rather than symptoms the patient reports.
Pruritus, pain and paresthesia
Correct — itch, pain and abnormal sensation are the three symptom categories.
Pruritus alone, since it is the commonest skin symptom
Pruritus is only one of them; pain and paresthesia are the other skin symptoms asked about when taking the history.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Which part of the examiner's hand should rest against the patient during otoscopy?
opts: The ulnar aspect
Correct. The ulnar aspect of the hand contacts the patient, anchoring the otoscope so a sudden movement does not drive it into the canal.
The palm, to steady the patient's head
The anchoring is of the instrument against the head, and it is the ulnar border of the hand that makes the contact.
The thumb, to hold the auricle in position
The other hand holds the auricle. The ulnar aspect of the otoscope hand makes the contact.
No part — the otoscope is held clear of the patient
Holding it clear is exactly what makes a sudden movement dangerous.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: What does a NORMAL lymph node feel like?
opts: Hard, fixed and irregular
Hard and fixed nodes suggest malignancy; a normal node is round or ovoid, smooth, mobile and non-tender.
Soft, tender and warm
A tender node suggests inflammation; a normal node is smooth, mobile and non-tender, round or ovoid.
Rubbery, matted and non-tender
