Color is a core characteristic; color, moisture, temperature, texture, mobility and turgor, and lesions are all assessed.
Thickness, elasticity and capillary refill time
Thickness and capillary refill are not assessed; the skin is checked for color, moisture, temperature, texture, mobility and turgor, and lesions.
Color, moisture, temperature, texture, mobility and turgor, and lesions
Correct — six characteristics, of which color and lesions begin with inspection and the remainder require touch.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: How does the course of CENTRAL vertigo differ in duration from the peripheral causes?
opts: Always under one minute
Episodes under one minute are the benign positional vertigo pattern; central vertigo is variable in duration.
Always several hours
Episodes of several hours to a day or more fit Ménière disease; central vertigo is variable and rarely continuous.
Variable, but rarely continuous
Correct. Central vertigo runs a variable course but is rarely continuous, whereas each peripheral cause has a characteristic duration.
Always continuous until treated
Central vertigo is variable but RARELY continuous, so a course that is always continuous does not fit it.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: FINE hair and COARSE hair on examination point to which conditions?
opts: Both to hypothyroidism
The two textures point in opposite directions: fine hair to hyperthyroidism, coarse hair to hypothyroidism.
Both to nutritional deficiency
Hair texture here reflects thyroid status: fine hair suggests hyperthyroidism, coarse hair hypothyroidism.
Fine hair to hyperthyroidism; coarse hair to hypothyroidism
Correct — a small finding, but it is examined for at the same moment as the scalp and the skull.
Fine hair to hypothyroidism; coarse hair to hyperthyroidism
Reversed: fine hair points to hyperthyroidism and coarse hair to hypothyroidism.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: How much difference in pupil size is common?
opts: It is benign only if both pupils are under three millimeters
Benign anisocoria depends on normal pupillary reactions, not absolute size; half to one millimeter of difference is common.
Half to one millimeter is common
Correct — a difference of half to one millimeter is common, and anisocoria is benign if the pupillary reactions are normal.
Any difference at all is abnormal
Small differences are common: half to one millimeter is normal, and a difference over 1 mm is abnormal.
Up to three millimeters is common
Three millimeters is too much; half to one millimeter is common, and more than 1 mm is abnormal.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 70

D.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
D.q: A palpable, elevated solid mass measuring less than one centimeter is called what?
opts: A papule
Correct — a papule is a palpable, elevated solid mass under one centimeter, as in nevi, warts and lichen planus.
A macule
A macule is a flat discoloration; a palpable, elevated solid mass under one centimeter is a papule.
A nodule
A nodule lies deeper in the dermis and is one to two centimeters.
A vesicle
A vesicle is a superficial elevation filled with fluid; a solid elevated mass under one centimeter is a papule.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: What does the crescent shadow test with oblique lighting assess?
opts: Pupil reactivity — a shadow means an afferent defect
Afferent defects are found with the swinging light test; the oblique light shadow reflects a narrow angle.
The depth of the anterior chamber angle
Correct — a shadow on the medial iris means it is bowed forward into a narrow angle, raising the risk of narrow-angle glaucoma.
Corneal clarity — a shadow means an epithelial defect
Areas of cornea devoid of epithelium are shown by fluorescein uptake; the oblique light shadow reflects a narrow angle.
Lens opacity — a shadow means cataract
Cataract is seen as a lens opacity through the pupil; the oblique light shadow reflects a narrow iris-cornea angle.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 90

D.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
D.q: Which areas of the scalp should be specifically inspected?
opts: The vertex and the temples
The vertex and temples are not singled out; after parting the hair, inspect behind the ears and the occiput.
The anterior hairline and the eyebrows
The hairline and eyebrows are not singled out; the areas to inspect specifically are behind the ears and the occiput.
The crown alone, since disease elsewhere is rare
Inspection is not limited to the crown; part the hair in sections and inspect behind the ears and the occiput.
Behind the ears and the occiput
Correct — these are the areas most easily missed if the hair is not parted.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: What does the cover-uncover test reveal?
opts: A field defect
Field defects are found by confrontation testing; the cover-uncover test reveals slight muscle imbalance.
A slight muscle imbalance not otherwise seen
Correct — the cover-uncover test may reveal a slight muscle imbalance not otherwise seen.
An afferent pupillary defect
An afferent pupillary defect is found with the swinging light test; cover-uncover reveals slight muscle imbalance.
A refractive error
Refractive error is shown by pinhole testing; the cover-uncover test reveals slight muscle imbalance.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 67

D.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
D.q: Which piece of equipment aids inspection when lice are suspected?
opts: A tongue depressor
A tongue depressor has no role here; a magnifying glass helps show nits as tiny white ovoid granules on the hairs.
A magnifying glass
Correct — nits appear as tiny white ovoid granules adherent to the hair shafts.
A Wood's lamp
A Wood's lamp is not the aid for lice; a magnifying glass shows nits as tiny white ovoid granules adhering to hairs.
A dermatoscope
A dermatoscope is not the aid for lice; a magnifying glass shows nits as tiny white ovoid granules adhering to hairs.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: Deep eye pain is associated with which condition?
opts: Blepharitis
Blepharitis is a common lid inflammation linked to bacterial infection or atopic dermatitis; deep pain points to angle closure.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Correct — deep eye pain is linked to acute narrow angle glaucoma; pain from a deeper source is not relieved by topical anesthetic.
Allergic conjunctivitis
Allergy shows itching and excessive tearing rather than deep pain, which is linked to acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Corneal abrasion
A corneal abrasion is a surface injury that feels better with topical anesthetic; deep pain points to acute narrow angle glaucoma.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 12

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: How does the SIZE of the striking object change the injury?
opts: Larger objects strike the globe directly; smaller objects hit the rim
This reverses the mechanics: smaller objects may strike the globe directly, while larger ones load the orbital rim.
Object size makes no difference
Size is important: it determines whether the periocular soft tissues or the globe itself is likely to be injured.
Only velocity matters, not size
Velocity matters for penetration, but size matters too: larger objects hit the orbital rim, smaller ones the globe.
Larger objects transfer most of the energy to the orbital rim
Correct — larger objects transfer most of their energy to the orbital rim, while smaller objects may strike the globe itself.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 111

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: What is inspected on the mucosa, tonsils and pharynx?
opts: Erythema, exudates, ulcerations and lesions
Correct — the four things being looked for every time, whatever the complaint.
Only exudates
Exudates are one of the four things looked for, alongside erythema, ulceration and other lesions.
Only the size of the tonsils
Tonsil size is not the focus; the mucosa, tonsils and pharynx are inspected for erythema, exudates, ulcerations and lesions.
Only the color of the mucosa
Erythema is only one of four; exudates, ulcerations and other lesions are inspected for as well.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: A patient says they are “dizzy”. Which four categories must the history separate?
opts: Vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium and psychiatric causes
Correct. The word means nothing until the patient explains it, and these are the four things it turns out to mean.
Vertigo, migraine, seizure and syncope
Migraine and seizure are not dizziness categories; the four are vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium and psychiatric causes.
Peripheral vertigo, central vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss
This splits vertigo into its own subtypes but omits the non-vestibular causes, which is the whole reason for asking.
Orthostatic, cardiac, neurological and metabolic
A reasonable clinical list, but it splits by mechanism rather than by what the patient is actually describing.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: What is geographic tongue?
opts: A fungal infection of the tongue
A fungal infection of the mouth is candidiasis; geographic tongue is benign and not an infection.
A benign map-like pattern of patches
Correct. Geographic tongue is a benign finding, so recognizing it mainly avoids mistaking it for something that needs investigation.
A premalignant lesion requiring biopsy
Geographic tongue is benign, not premalignant, so biopsy is not what the finding calls for.
A sign of vitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency gives a smooth, beefy red tongue; geographic tongue is a benign finding.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: The tongue deviates to one side on protrusion. Which nerve is involved?
opts: Cranial nerve XII
Correct. Asymmetric protrusion is the hypoglossal sign, and it is why the tongue is checked for midline position.
Cranial nerve X
Cranial nerve X gives uvular deviation and failure of the palate to rise.
Cranial nerve V
The trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication, not the tongue.
Cranial nerve VII
Cranial nerve VII is not tested by tongue protrusion; asymmetric protrusion is the sign of a cranial nerve XII lesion.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: What is tinnitus, by definition?
opts: A perception of rotation or spinning
A perception of rotation, spinning or tilting defines vertigo; tinnitus is a sound with no external source.
Hearing loss confined to the high frequencies
Higher frequency loss is the presbycusis pattern, a sensorineural loss; tinnitus is a perceived sound, not a loss.
A sensation of fullness or pressure in the ear
Aural fullness — a separate symptom, though it accompanies tinnitus in Ménière disease.
Sound perceived with no external source
Correct. The definition turns on the absence of an external stimulus, which is what separates it from any complaint about external sound.

D.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
D.q: Round scaling patches of alopecia with hairs broken off close to the scalp describe which infection?
opts: Tinea capitis
Correct — the broken hairs distinguish it from other causes of patchy hair loss.
Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata produces smooth patches with exclamation point hairs and no scaling.
Trichotillomania
Trichotillomania results from pulling and does not produce scaling patches.
Androgenic alopecia
Androgenic alopecia follows a male pattern rather than producing round scaling patches.

D.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
D.q: A palpable, elevated solid mass greater than two centimeters is called what?
opts: A cyst
A cyst is encapsulated and filled with liquid or semisolid material.
A tumor
Correct — a tumor is a palpable, elevated solid mass greater than two centimeters, such as a neoplasm.
A plaque
A plaque is plateau-like and over one centimeter; a solid elevated mass greater than two centimeters is a tumor.
A nodule
A nodule measures one to two centimeters; a solid elevated mass greater than two centimeters is a tumor.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: How is the kinetic red target test performed?
opts: Wiggle the fingers and bring them into view
Wiggling fingers into view is the static finger wiggle test; the kinetic test uses a 5 mm red-topped pin.
Ask the patient to count fingers at each quadrant
Counting fingers is not this test; the kinetic test moves a 5 mm red pin inward and asks when it first looks red.
Move a 5 mm red-topped pin inward from beyond the boundary of each quadrant along a line bisecting the meridians, and ask when the pin first appears RED
Correct — a 5 mm red-topped pin moves inward along lines bisecting the meridians, and the endpoint is when it first appears red.
Move a white target inward and ask when it is first seen at all
The target is a 5 mm red-topped pin, and the endpoint is when it first appears red, not when it is first seen.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 54

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: Which failure would make an infectious red eye worse?
opts: Failing to recognize an infectious cause and inappropriately prescribing topical corticosteroid drops
Correct — missing an infectious cause of red eye and prescribing topical corticosteroid drops is a common examination mistake.
Failing to measure the intraocular pressure
Ocular pressure is checked only if it can be done accurately and safely; the infection risk comes from steroid drops.
Failing to dilate the pupil
Primary care clinicians do not dilate most patients; the mistake that harms an infected eye is prescribing steroid drops.
Failing to document the family history
The eye findings are what must be documented; prescribing steroid drops is the mistake that worsens an infection.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 20

D.io: a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
D.q: Which of the following is a function of the skin?
opts: Production of vitamin D
Correct. The skin also protects internal structures, prevents entry of microorganisms, regulates temperature and participates in excretion.
Production of clotting factors
Clotting factors are synthesized by the liver, not the skin.
Storage of calcium for release into the blood
Calcium storage is not a skin function; the skin protects, blocks microorganisms, regulates temperature, excretes and produces vitamin D.
Filtration of nitrogenous waste from the blood
That is renal work; the skin's excretory role is limited to what leaves in sweat.

D.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
D.q: When asking about medications in a dermatological history, what must be included?
opts: Only medications applied directly to the affected skin
Topical agents are not the focus; the history asks about systemic medications, both over-the-counter and prescription.
Only medications started within the past week
No time window limits the question; every systemic medication, over-the-counter and prescription, should be asked about.
Both over-the-counter and prescription systemic medications
Correct — limiting the question to prescriptions misses a large share of drug eruptions.
Only prescription medications, since these are the ones documented in the chart
Over-the-counter medications must be asked about as well as prescriptions, since both kinds of systemic medication are covered.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
D.q: In acute glaucoma, what is the pupil like?
opts: May be small and, with time, irregular
A small pupil that may become irregular is acute iritis; in acute glaucoma the pupil is dilated and fixed.
Not affected unless iritis develops
A pupil spared unless iritis develops is corneal injury or infection; in acute glaucoma it is dilated and fixed.
Dilated and fixed
Correct — acute glaucoma gives a dilated, fixed pupil, with a steamy cornea and an acute rise in intraocular pressure.
Not affected
An unaffected pupil belongs to conjunctivitis and subconjunctival hemorrhage; in acute glaucoma it is dilated and fixed.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: How are the frontal and maxillary sinuses palpated?
opts: Press UP on both, avoiding the eyes
Correct. Both the frontal and the maxillary sinuses are pressed upward, and the frontal sinuses are pressed while avoiding the eyes.
Press DOWN on the frontal sinuses and down on the maxillary sinuses
The direction for both sinuses is upward, not downward, with care to avoid the eyes over the frontal sinuses.
Press directly on the globes to assess the frontal sinuses
The eyes must be avoided, not pressed; the frontal sinuses are palpated by pressing upward while avoiding the eyes.
Percuss both sinuses with a reflex hammer
The sinuses are palpated by pressing upward for pain or tenderness, not percussed with a reflex hammer.

D.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
D.q: Which term describes a ring-shaped lesion?
opts: Annular
Correct — annular lesions are shaped like a ring, as distinct from arcs (arciform) or coils (gyrate).
Arciform
Arciform lesions form arcs or curves rather than complete rings.
Reticular
Reticular describes a lacy or networked pattern; a lesion shaped like a ring is called annular.
Gyrate
Gyrate means twisted, coiled, spiral or snakelike; a lesion shaped like a ring is called annular.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: What does bleeding of the gums suggest?
opts: Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis only
That is a specific severe entity; ordinary bleeding gums point to gingivitis generally.
Oral carcinoma
Oral cancer presents as an indurated red or white lesion, usually lateral or under the tongue.
Gingivitis
Correct. Bleeding gums point to gingivitis — inflammation of the gum margin itself.
Vitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency shows as a smooth, beefy red tongue, not bleeding gums, which point to gingivitis.

D.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
D.q: Fine, irregular blood vessels that blanch under pressure are called what?
opts: Spider angiomas
A spider angioma has a central red macule with radiating arms.
Cherry angiomas
A cherry angioma is a dome-shaped, bright red to violet lesion; fine, irregular blanching vessels are telangiectasias.
Telangiectasias
Correct — blanching confirms the blood remains within vessels.
Petechiae
Petechiae are tiny non-blanching macules; fine, irregular vessels that blanch are telangiectasias.

D.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
D.q: What does the term confluent mean when applied to skin lesions?
opts: The lesions form a line or stripe
Lesions forming a line or stripe are linear; confluent means the lesions run together.
The lesions run together
Correct — the opposite of discrete, where lesions remain separate.
The lesions remain separate from one another
Lesions that remain separate are discrete; confluent lesions are the opposite, running together.
The lesions form a cluster
A cluster of lesions is described as grouped; confluent means the lesions run together.

D.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
D.q: An enlarged supraclavicular node on the LEFT. What does it suggest?
opts: Local infection of the scalp
Scalp infection drains to the occipital and postauricular nodes.
Dental infection
Dental infection drains to the submandibular and submental nodes.
Tonsillitis
Tonsillar infection drains to the tonsillar and anterior cervical nodes.
Metastasis from an abdominal or thoracic malignancy
Correct. The left supraclavicular node drains territory far from the neck, so finding one there redirects the whole search.

D.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
D.q: What distinguishes a nodule from a papule?
opts: A nodule is transient while a papule persists
Transience is the defining feature of a wheal, not a nodule.
A nodule is deeper in the dermis and measures one to two centimeters
Correct — depth as well as size separates the two; basal cell carcinoma and neurofibromatosis are examples of nodules.
A nodule is fluid-filled while a papule is solid
Both are solid; a nodule differs from a papule by lying deeper in the dermis and measuring one to two centimeters.
A nodule is flat while a papule is elevated
Both are elevated; a nodule lies deeper in the dermis than a papule and measures one to two centimeters.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Which causes produce CENTRAL vertigo?
opts: Otitis media, otitis externa and Eustachian tube dysfunction
Middle and external ear disease — these cause ear pain, not central vertigo.
Brainstem lesion, atherosclerosis and multiple sclerosis
Correct — all vascular, demyelinating or structural problems above the inner ear, with vertebrobasilar migraine and transient ischemic attack completing the list.
Benign positional vertigo, Ménière disease and labyrinthitis
Benign positional vertigo, Ménière disease and labyrinthitis are all peripheral causes arising in the inner ear.
Loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, salicylates and alcohol
Loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, salicylates and alcohol cause drug toxicity vertigo, which is a peripheral cause.

E.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
E.q: The memory aid "bugs, drugs, contact" prompts you to ask about which three areas?
opts: Insect bites, antibiotic allergies, and the use of gloves at work
Insect bites and glove use are single examples; the three areas are contacts and travel, systemic medications, and allergens or irritants.
Bacterial cultures, prescription records, and patch testing results
Cultures, records and patch tests are investigations; the aid prompts history questions on contacts and travel, medications and allergens.
Pets in the home, over-the-counter creams, and laundry detergent brand
Examples of each category, but not the categories themselves.
Affected family members or contacts and travel, systemic medications
Correct — bugs (affected family, contacts, travel), drugs (systemic medications) and contact (allergens or irritants from hobbies, occupation or environment).

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Which conditions cause proptosis or exophthalmos?
opts: Conjunctivitis and episcleritis
Those inflame the surface of the eye; proptosis signals orbital disease such as retrobulbar hemorrhage or Graves disease.
Retrobulbar hemorrhage, orbital cellulitis, orbital tumor, and Graves disease
Correct — proptosis signals orbital disease: retrobulbar hemorrhage, orbital cellulitis, orbital tumor or Graves disease.
Cataract, glaucoma and macular degeneration
Those cause visual loss from within the eye; forward displacement signals orbital disease such as Graves disease or a tumor.
Blepharitis, chalazion and hordeolum
Those are eyelid lesions; forward displacement of the eye signals orbital disease such as orbital cellulitis or a tumor.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 24

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: A patient has intact skin over the sacrum with an area of erythema that fails to blanch with pressure. What stage of pressure ulcer is this?
opts: Stage I
Correct — the skin is still intact, and the non-blanching erythema is the key finding.
Stage II
Stage II is partial thickness skin loss; intact skin with non-blanching erythema is stage I.
Stage III
Stage III involves full thickness skin loss with necrosis of subcutaneous tissue.
Stage IV
Stage IV destroys tissue, muscle and bone; intact skin with non-blanching erythema is stage I.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: What are the fundoscopic findings in papilledema?
opts: A white disc with absent tiny vessels — from death of optic nerve fibers
A white disc with absent tiny vessels is optic atrophy; papilledema is a pink swollen disc with blurred margins.
An enlarged cup more than half the disc diameter — from raised intraocular pressure
An enlarged cup over half the disc is glaucomatous cupping; papilledema is a swollen disc in which the cup is not visible.
Cotton-wool patches and hard exudates — from diabetes
Cotton-wool patches and hard exudates are retinal lesions of diabetes and hypertension; papilledema is a swollen pink disc.
A pink swollen disc with blurred margins and no visible cup, with loss of vessel pulsations
Correct — increased intracranial pressure swells the disc: pink, margins blurred, cup not visible, vessel pulsations lost.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 103

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: A green discoloration of the nail suggests infection with which organism?
opts: Candida
This organism is associated with chronic paronychia rather than green nails.
Pseudomonas
Correct — the pigment it produces gives the nail its green color.
A dermatophyte fungus
Fungal nail infection is tinea unguium and does not produce green discoloration.
Staphylococcus aureus
This organism causes acute paronychia rather than green nail discoloration.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: What does the pinhole test distinguish?
opts: An afferent from an efferent pupil defect
Afferent defects are found with the swinging light test; the pinhole separates refractive error from other causes of poor acuity.
A refractive error from other causes
Correct — a pinhole passes only light perpendicular to the lens, so a deficit it corrects is refractive; if not, consider cataract or nerve disease.
Glaucoma from cataract, by measuring pressure indirectly
The pinhole does not measure pressure, which is the tonometer pen's job; it separates refractive error from other causes.
A field defect from an acuity problem, by isolating quadrants
Fields are tested by confrontation; the pinhole is an acuity test that separates refractive error from other causes.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 52

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Which findings suggest a zygomatic fracture?
opts: A sunken eye with diplopia on upward gaze
A sunken eye with diplopia on upward gaze points to an orbital floor fracture; the zygoma shows a flattened cheek.
Proptosis with restricted painful movement
Proptosis signals orbital disease such as cellulitis or tumor; a zygomatic fracture flattens the cheek instead.
A 360-degree subconjunctival hemorrhage
Hemorrhage encircling the cornea after trauma raises concern for globe rupture; a zygomatic fracture flattens the cheek.
Flattening of the malar eminence best seen from behind the seated patient looking down, edema and ecchymosis of the temple or infraorbital area, and a palpable step-off on palpating the zygoma
Correct — a zygomatic fracture flattens the malar eminence, seen from behind, with temple or infraorbital swelling and a palpable step-off.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 117

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: Spoon-shaped concave nails in which the nail plate thins and becomes inverted are called what?
opts: Nail pitting
Nail pitting is small depressions in the nail plate; a spoon-shaped, concave, inverted nail is koilonychia.
Koilonychia
Correct — the concavity is deep enough that the nail can hold a drop of water.
Onycholysis
Onycholysis is painless separation of the nail plate from the nail bed.
Clubbing
Clubbing produces a rounded, bulbous fingertip with an increased nail base angle.

E.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
E.q: A patient with atopic dermatitis has thickened skin with accentuated skin lines from years of scratching. What is this called?
opts: Collarette scaling
Collarette scale is a peripherally attached, centrally detached scale at a lesion's edge.
Lichenification
Correct — lichenification is a secondary lesion of thickening with accentuated skin lines caused by chronic irritation.
Keloid formation
A keloid is a scar that grows beyond the wound; thickening with accentuated skin lines is lichenification.
Callus formation
A callus is thickened epidermal keratin from repetitive pressure, typically on the sole.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: A BLUE sclera indicates what?
opts: Osteogenesis imperfecta
Correct — a blue sclera is the scleral color seen in osteogenesis imperfecta.
Liver disease
Liver disease gives a yellow sclera through jaundice; a blue sclera is seen in osteogenesis imperfecta.
Thyroid eye disease
Thyroid eye disease causes proptosis and lid lag, not scleral color; a blue sclera suggests osteogenesis imperfecta.
Long-term steroid use
Steroid use is a cataract risk factor, not a cause of scleral color; a blue sclera suggests osteogenesis imperfecta.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 43

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Which pair of diagnoses must be differentiated because the latter can lead to death?
opts: Cataract from glaucoma
Simple glaucoma and cataract both cause gradual painless loss; the pair that matters because one can kill is preseptal versus orbital cellulitis.
Hordeolum from chalazion
A hordeolum is a painful lid-margin infection and a chalazion a painless nodule; the pair that matters is preseptal versus orbital cellulitis.
Preseptal from orbital cellulitis
Correct — preseptal cellulitis must be told apart from orbital cellulitis, because orbital cellulitis can lead to death.
Episcleritis from scleritis
Nodular episcleritis goes with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus; the pair that matters because one can kill is preseptal versus orbital cellulitis.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 20

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: How is a fluorescein stain performed?
opts: The dye changes the color of the aqueous humor
The dye is placed on the eye and viewed under blue light, where areas of cornea without epithelium take it up.
Orange dye is instilled and a blue light used
Correct — orange dye goes into the eye and a blue light shows foreign bodies or corneal damage, since bare areas take up the dye.
The dye stains intact epithelium and spares defects
It is the reverse: the dye is taken up by areas of cornea devoid of epithelium, lit with a blue light.
The dye is injected and photographed with a blue flash
The dye is placed in the eye, not injected; a blue light then shows foreign bodies or corneal damage.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 121

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Which three findings together describe the tympanic membrane in acute otitis media?
opts: Red, retracted, and with the landmarks exaggerated
Retraction with exaggerated landmarks is the opposite picture — negative middle ear pressure pulling the membrane inward.
Pale, thickened and immobile
Thickening describes chronic change; the acute picture is redness and bulging.
Amber with visible bubbles
That is a serous effusion, without the redness of acute infection.
Red, bulging, and with the landmarks lost
Correct. The purulent effusion behind it pushes it outward and obscures the normal anatomy.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Eye pain WITH HEADACHE suggests what?
opts: Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis pairs eye pain with a gritty feeling; eye pain with headache suggests acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Correct — eye pain together with headache is the pairing for acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Corneal abrasion or foreign body
A corneal abrasion or foreign body hurts with blinking; eye pain with headache suggests acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis causes pain on eye motion; eye pain with headache suggests acute narrow angle glaucoma.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 17

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: What is needed to inspect the POSTERIOR pharynx properly?
opts: A tongue blade
Correct. The tongue obscures the posterior wall and has to be depressed out of the way.
An otoscope with the largest speculum
The otoscope examines the ear canal; the posterior pharynx may need a tongue blade to move the tongue aside.
A nasal speculum
A nasal speculum is for the nose; inspecting the posterior pharynx may require a tongue blade instead.
Transillumination in a dark room
Transillumination in a dark room is the sinus technique; the posterior pharynx is viewed with a tongue blade.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Entropion and ectropion both affect which eyelid?
opts: The upper lid
Both malpositions affect the lower lid: entropion folds it inward and ectropion turns it outward.
Both lids equally
They do not affect both lids equally; entropion and ectropion are both lower lid malpositions.
Neither — they affect the conjunctiva
They are lid malpositions, not conjunctival disease: entropion turns the lower lid in, ectropion turns it out.
The lower lid
Correct — entropion is inward folding and ectropion outward turning, and both affect the lower lid.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 3

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: What is hyperemia?
opts: Injection of the superficially visible vessels of the conjunctiva, episclera or sclera
Correct — hyperemia is injection of the superficially visible vessels of the conjunctiva, episclera or sclera.
Swelling of the conjunctiva
That is chemosis, swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva; hyperemia is injection of the superficial visible vessels.
Blood collecting beneath the conjunctiva
That is a subconjunctival hemorrhage, blood leaking outside the vessels; hyperemia is injection of the visible vessels.
Inward folding of the lower lid
That is entropion, inward folding of the lower lid; hyperemia is injection of the superficially visible vessels.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 3

E.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
E.q: Lesions confined to sun-exposed skin should raise concern for which condition?
opts: Intertrigo
Intertrigo occurs in skin folds, which are shielded from the sun.
Herpes zoster
Herpes zoster follows a dermatome rather than sun exposure; lesions confined to sun-exposed skin suggest skin cancers.
Psoriasis
Psoriasis favors extensor surfaces rather than sun-exposed skin specifically.
Skin cancers
Correct — cumulative ultraviolet exposure explains why these arise where the sun reaches.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: When is globe rupture more likely in a patient with a subconjunctival hemorrhage?
opts: When the hemorrhage is small and sectoral
A small patch is the usually harmless picture; rupture is more likely when the hemorrhage encircles the entire cornea after trauma.
When the patient is anticoagulated
A bleeding disorder can cause the hemorrhage, but rupture is signaled by trauma with blood encircling the entire cornea.
When both eyes are affected
Bilaterality is not the warning sign; rupture is more likely with trauma and hemorrhage encircling the entire cornea.
In trauma, and when the hemorrhage encircles the entire cornea
Correct — globe rupture is more likely after trauma and when the hemorrhage encircles the entire cornea.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 44

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: Transverse depressions in the fingernail found halfway up the nail suggest what?
opts: Chronic hypoxia from lung disease
Lung disease is not what these lines record; transverse depressions halfway up the nail date an illness to about three months ago.
Iron deficiency of long standing
Iron deficiency is not what they record; Beau's lines halfway up the nail point to an illness about three months ago.
An illness about three months previously
Correct — these are Beau's lines, and the position on the nail dates the insult.
An illness within the past two weeks
A recent illness would not yet have grown out to the middle of the nail.

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: What distinguishes terminal hair from vellus hair?
opts: Terminal hair is short and fine while vellus hair is coarse
The descriptions are reversed: vellus hair is short and fine and covers the body, while terminal hair is coarse.
Terminal hair grows only after puberty while vellus hair is present only in infancy
Both are present throughout life in their respective distributions.
Terminal hair is pigmented while vellus hair is always white
Pigment does not separate them; terminal hair is coarse in specific areas, and vellus hair is short and fine over the body.
Terminal hair is coarse and grows on the scalp and in the pubic
Correct — terminal hair is coarse (scalp, pubic, axillary and beard areas), while vellus hair is short and fine and covers the body.

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: Painless separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, beginning distally, is called what?
opts: Onycholysis
Correct — onycholysis is painless separation that starts distally, and several or all nails are usually affected.
Koilonychia
Koilonychia is a spoon-shaped concave nail; painless separation of the plate from the bed is onycholysis.
Paronychia
Paronychia is soft tissue infection around the nail; painless plate separation from the bed is onycholysis.
Subungual hematoma
A subungual hematoma is hemorrhage to the nail plate; painless separation of the plate is onycholysis.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Which pairing of usual cause and accompanying finding fits a tympanic membrane perforation?
opts: Otitis media, and drainage may come through the perforation
Correct. The perforation is usually the consequence of middle ear disease rather than a primary event.
Otitis externa, with itching through the perforation
Otitis externa is confined to the canal and does not perforate the membrane.
Barotrauma, with vertigo through the perforation
Atmospheric pressure change brings on serous effusion; perforation usually follows otitis media, with drainage through it.
Cerumen impaction, with pain through the perforation
Cerumen blocks the canal and does not perforate the membrane; perforation usually follows otitis media, with drainage.

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: A patient has hair loss in multiple round patches with hairs that taper toward the scalp. What is the likely diagnosis?
opts: Androgenic alopecia
Androgenic alopecia follows a male pattern rather than producing discrete round patches.
Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis produces scaling patches with hairs broken off close to the scalp.
Trichotillomania
Trichotillomania results from pulling and does not produce exclamation point hairs.
Alopecia areata
Correct — these exclamation point hairs, along with round patches, characterize this chronic inflammatory disease of hair follicles.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: How long does benign positional vertigo last overall, as opposed to how long a single episode lasts?
opts: Each episode is under a minute, and the condition resolves within 24 hours
Too short. Benign positional vertigo lasts a few weeks rather than a day, and it may recur after settling.
Episodes last hours, and the condition lasts a few weeks
Episodes lasting several hours or more fit Ménière disease; a benign positional vertigo episode is under a minute.
Episodes and the condition both last a few weeks
The defining feature of positional vertigo is precisely how BRIEF each episode is.
Each episode is under a minute, but the condition lasts a few weeks and may recur
Correct. Each episode comes on over a few seconds to under a minute, but the condition itself lasts a few weeks and may recur.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: What is the rule about topical anesthetic in corneal abrasion?
opts: It should never be used at all
It is used, but for diagnosis: topical anesthetic brings immediate relief of an abrasion and is not a treatment.
It is only useful if the cornea is hazy
A hazy cornea suggests bacterial infection; topical anesthetic is used for diagnosis of an abrasion, not treatment.
Use it for diagnosis, not as a treatment
Correct — topical anesthetic brings immediate relief of an abrasion, but it is used for diagnosis and not as a treatment.
It should be prescribed for home use to control pain
It is not a take-home treatment; topical anesthetic in abrasion is used for diagnosis only, despite the immediate relief.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 120

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Which list contains only CONDUCTIVE causes of hearing loss?
opts: Rubella, cytomegalovirus and hereditary loss
Rubella, cytomegalovirus and hereditary loss are sensorineural causes arising in the inner ear, not conductive ones.
Cerumen, foreign bodies, effusions, exostoses, tumors and tympanic membrane perforation
Correct. Every one of them obstructs or loads the external or middle ear.
Presbycusis, noise exposure, acoustic neuroma and Ménière disease
Presbycusis, noise exposure, acoustic neuroma and Ménière disease are all sensorineural, inner ear causes.
Cerumen, presbycusis, effusions and noise exposure
A mixed list: presbycusis and noise exposure are sensorineural.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Which description of the nasolacrimal duct obstruction test is correct?
opts: Evert the upper lid and inspect the tarsal conjunctiva
Lid eversion is the search for a foreign body; the duct test compresses the lacrimal sac and watches the puncta.

Ask the patient to look up, press on the lower lid near the medial canthus just inside the bony orbit to compress the lacrimal sac, and look for fluid regurgitating from the puncta — mucopurulent fluid suggests obstruction
Correct — compressing the lacrimal sac near the medial canthus and seeing mucopurulent fluid from the puncta suggests an obstructed duct.
Instill fluorescein and time its disappearance from the tear film
Fluorescein is used to show corneal damage under blue light; the duct test compresses the lacrimal sac and watches the puncta.
Press on the upper lid near the lateral canthus and look for tearing
The press is on the lower lid near the medial canthus, over the lacrimal sac, watching for fluid from the puncta.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 38

E.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
E.q: Which term describes a lacy or networked pattern of lesions?
opts: Reticular
Correct — reticular describes a lacy or networked pattern, as opposed to a line (linear) or arcs (arciform).
Linear
Linear lesions form a line or stripe; a lacy or networked pattern is described as reticular.
Gyrate
Gyrate lesions are twisted, coiled or spiral; a lacy or networked pattern is described as reticular.
Arciform
Arciform lesions form arcs or curves; a lacy or networked pattern is described as reticular.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Once local eye disease is excluded, which of these remains a cause of a dilated pupil?
opts: Optic neuritis, papilledema and optic atrophy
Optic nerve disease affects the afferent limb; the remaining causes are a third nerve lesion, an Adie's pupil or pharmacologic block.
Compression or other lesion of the third cranial nerve
Correct — the three remaining causes are a third nerve lesion, ciliary ganglion damage causing Adie's pupil, and pharmacologic sphincter block.
Glaucoma, cataract and macular degeneration
Those are local eye diseases, already excluded; what remains is a third nerve lesion, an Adie's pupil or a pharmacologic block.
Horner syndrome, myasthenia gravis and Graves disease
Horner syndrome gives a SMALL pupil; what remains is a third nerve lesion, an Adie's pupil or a pharmacologic block.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 86

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: A raised, shiny, slow-growing lesion on the auricle with visible telangiectasia. What should be suspected?
opts: A cutaneous cyst
A cutaneous cyst is benign, usually epidermoid or pilar; raised, shiny and telangiectatic points to basal cell carcinoma.
A keloid
Scar tissue, typically at a site of previous injury or piercing.
A tophus
A tophus is a hard uric acid nodule of chronic tophaceous gout, not a shiny lesion with telangiectasia.
Basal cell carcinoma
Correct. Raised, shiny, telangiectatic and slow growing — and malignant, which is what separates it from the benign lumps in the same list.

E.io: g — Documentation of a complete history and physical examination
E.q: How should subjective and objective information be arranged in a note?
opts: Subjective information may be omitted when the examination is complete
Both are required regardless of how complete the examination was.
Objective findings recorded within the assessment section
Objective findings do not belong in the assessment; they are kept in the objective section, separate from subjective information.
Each kept in its own appropriate section, not mixed together
Correct — subjective and objective information are each kept in their appropriate sections of the note rather than blended.
Combined into a single narrative so the encounter reads chronologically
A single chronological narrative mixes the two; subjective and objective information each belong in their own appropriate section.
E.cite: Intro to PD II - Elwaya .pdf, Page 20

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: An abnormally ENLARGED head raises which two conditions?
opts: Hypothyroidism and acromegaly
Hypothyroidism and acromegaly are not causes of an enlarged head; those are hydrocephalus and Paget disease.
Paget disease and microcephaly
Microcephaly belongs with a small head, not an enlarged one, which raises hydrocephalus and Paget disease.
Hydrocephalus and Paget disease
Correct. One expands the skull from within, the other thickens the bone itself.
Microcephaly and hydrocephalus
Microcephaly is an abnormally small head; an enlarged head raises hydrocephalus and Paget disease.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Which corneal ulcer is NOT very painful?
opts: Bacterial corneal ulcers
Bacterial ulcers cause pain, photophobia and tearing; it is herpes simplex ulcers that are not very painful.
Fungal corneal ulcers
Fungal ulcers share the usual pain and photophobia; it is herpes simplex ulcers that are not very painful.
Amoebic corneal ulcers
Amoebic ulcers share the usual pain and photophobia; it is herpes simplex ulcers that are not very painful.
Herpes simplex corneal ulcers
Correct — corneal ulcers usually bring pain and photophobia, but herpes simplex corneal ulcers are not very painful.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 122

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Which epistaxis history suggests a SYSTEMIC problem rather than a local one?
opts: Bleeding that follows a recent upper respiratory infection
Inflammation after an infection is a local cause of epistaxis, like trauma, dry mucosa, a foreign body or a tumor.
Bleeding in dry winter air
Dry mucosa is a local cause; a systemic problem is suggested by recurrent bleeding or bleeding and bruising elsewhere.
Recurrent bleeding, or bleeding and bruising elsewhere on the body
Correct. One nosebleed is local until proven otherwise; a pattern of bleeding at other sites changes the question entirely.
Bleeding from one nostril after digital trauma
Bleeding after digital trauma is a local cause; recurrence, or bleeding and bruising elsewhere, suggests a systemic problem.

E.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
E.q: Which descriptive terms are used for skin moisture?
opts: Dryness, sweating and oiliness
Correct — dryness, sweating and oiliness are the terms used to describe skin moisture on examination.
Roughness and smoothness
Roughness and smoothness describe texture; moisture is described as dryness, sweating or oiliness.
Warmth and coolness
Warmth and coolness describe temperature; moisture is described as dryness, sweating or oiliness.
Mobility and turgor
Those are assessed by lifting a fold of skin and are separate from moisture.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Where does a chalazion usually point?
opts: At the medial canthus
The medial canthus is where the lacrimal sac is compressed; a chalazion usually points inside the lid, not at a canthus.
At the lateral canthus
A chalazion does not point to the lateral canthus; it usually points inside the lid rather than on the lid margin.
Inside the lid rather than on the lid margin
Correct — a chalazion, a nodule of a blocked meibomian gland, usually points inside the lid rather than on the lid margin.
On the lid margin at the lash line
The lid margin is where a hordeolum sits; a chalazion usually points inside the lid rather than on the margin.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 33

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is known by which other names?
opts: Aphthous stomatitis, and canker sores
Canker sores are aphthous ulcers; necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is also called Vincent's angina or trench mouth.
Vincent's angina, and trench mouth
Correct. Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is also called Vincent's angina or trench mouth, a painful, severe gum infection with rapid tissue death.
Ludwig's angina, and quinsy
Ludwig's angina is a floor-of-mouth cellulitis; quinsy is a peritonsillar abscess.
Angular cheilitis, and perleche
Angular cheilitis is cracking at the corners of the mouth; this gingivitis is also called Vincent's angina or trench mouth.

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: A translucent, pearly nodule with a depressed center and raised borders on the face is characteristic of which malignancy?
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma appears as a red scaling, crusting nodule or plaque.
Malignant melanoma
Melanoma appears as an irregularly colored plaque with sharp notches and variation of pigment.
Kaposi's sarcoma
Kaposi's sarcoma produces dark blue-purple lesions, most often in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
Basal cell carcinoma
Correct — it may ulcerate, and a non-healing ulcer on the face should raise the same suspicion.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: How is the RINNE test performed, in order?
opts: Fork on the mastoid until the sound stops, then beside the canal
Correct. Bone conduction comes first, with the fork on the mastoid until the sound stops; the fork then moves close to the canal and the patient is asked if it is still heard.
Fork close to the canal first, then on the mastoid once the sound stops
The sequence starts at the mastoid, testing bone conduction first.
Fork on the vertex of the head, then moved to the mastoid
The top of the head is where the Weber fork goes; Rinne starts on the mastoid and then moves close to the canal.
Fork held in front of both ears simultaneously
Rinne tests one ear at a time and compares two positions on that ear.

E.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
E.q: Which term describes lesions clustered in a dermatomal distribution?
opts: Herpetiform
Herpetiform describes grouping like herpes simplex rather than a dermatomal band.
Serpiginous
Serpiginous describes a snake-like lesion; lesions clustered in a dermatomal distribution are zosteriform.
Iris
Iris describes a target or bull's-eye shape; lesions clustered along a dermatome are zosteriform.
Zosteriform
Correct — zosteriform lesions cluster in a dermatomal distribution, the pattern seen in herpes zoster.

E.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
E.q: A lesion with a central red macule and radiating spider-like arms that blanches is called what?
opts: A spider angioma
Correct — the radiating arms and blanching together identify it.
A cherry angioma
A cherry angioma is dome-shaped and bright red to violet or black.
A telangiectasia
A telangiectasia consists of fine irregular vessels without a central macule.
Purpura
Purpura is a non-blanching reddish-purple macule; a blanching lesion with radiating arms is a spider angioma.

E.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
E.q: Which finding is described by the term rubor?
opts: Loss of normal skin color
Loss of normal color is pallor, a separate color finding; rubor is erythema, meaning redness of the skin.
A bluish discoloration of the skin
A bluish discoloration is cyanosis, central or peripheral; rubor is erythema, meaning redness of the skin.
Erythema, or redness of the skin
Correct — rubor and erythema are used interchangeably for redness.
Yellowing of the skin and sclerae
Yellowing is jaundice, a separate color finding; rubor is erythema, meaning redness of the skin.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: How does a septal hematoma form?
opts: Blood collects within the cartilage itself
Blood does not collect inside the cartilage; it collects between the septal lining and the cartilage beneath it.
Chronic inflammation erodes the septum until it bleeds
Erosion through the septum describes a perforation, caused by trauma, surgery or drug use, not a hematoma.
Venous engorgement of the turbinates spreads to the septum
Turbinate engorgement is not the mechanism; a hematoma is blood collecting between the septal lining and the cartilage.
Injured vessels bleed between the lining and the cartilage
Correct. Injury disrupts the blood vessels and pulls the lining away from the cartilage, allowing blood to collect between the two.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Which peripheral vertigo has sudden onset lasting hours to two weeks, with hearing unaffected and tinnitus absent?
opts: Benign positional vertigo
Benign positional vertigo comes in episodes of seconds to under a minute, set off by rolling over or tilting the head up.
Drug toxicity
Onset is insidious or acute and tied to a drug, and hearing may be impaired.
Vestibular neuronitis
Correct, and it may recur over twelve to eighteen months. Nausea, vomiting and nystagmus accompany it. Also called acute labyrinthitis.
Ménière disease
Hearing loss recurs and eventually progresses in Ménière, and tinnitus is present and fluctuating.

E.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
E.q: A collection of cellular debris, dried serum and blood forming a scab is called what?
opts: A crust
Correct — the antecedent primary lesion is usually a vesicle, bulla or pustule.
A scale
A scale is a thin flake of exfoliated epidermis; dried serum, blood and cellular debris form a crust.
An erosion
An erosion is a loss of superficial epidermis with a moist surface.
A fissure
A fissure is a linear crack in the skin; a scab of dried serum, blood and cellular debris is a crust.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Hard nodules on the auricle made of uric acid crystals. Which interpretation is correct?
opts: Cutaneous cysts, indicating follicular obstruction
Cutaneous cysts are benign epidermoid or pilar cysts, not crystal deposits; uric acid nodules are tophi of gout.
Exostoses, indicating repeated cold water exposure
Exostoses are bony growths in the canal, not nodules on the auricle.
Tophi, indicating chronic tophaceous gout
Correct. They are deposits rather than growths, and finding them on the ear points to long-standing disease.
Keloids, indicating previous trauma
Keloids are scar tissue, often at piercing sites, and contain no crystal; uric acid nodules are tophi of gout.

E.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and color
E.q: A thin flake of exfoliated epidermis, as seen in dandruff, is called what?
opts: A plaque
A plaque is a primary lesion, an elevated plateau-like mass.
Lichenification
Lichenification is thickening of the epidermis with accentuated skin lines.
A scale
Correct — a scale is a thin flake of exfoliated epidermis, as in dandruff or cradle cap.
A crust
A crust is dried serum, blood and cellular debris rather than shed epidermis.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: What is a NORMAL Weber result?
opts: Midline, or heard equally in both ears
Correct. There is no lateralization to report when both sides transmit equally.
Lateralized to the right
Any lateralization is abnormal in a patient with unilateral loss.
Heard only through bone conduction
Weber is a bone conduction test throughout; the finding is where the sound goes, not how it travels.
Not heard at all
A normal patient hears the tone, and it sits in the midline or is heard in both ears equally.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Which headache history suggests a MASS?
opts: Episodic and unilateral
Episodic and unilateral fits migraine or cluster headache, not the new, progressive, persistent headache of a mass.
Bilateral and band-like
Bilateral band-like pain is not the mass pattern; a mass causes a headache that is new, progressive and persistent.
New, progressive and persistent
Correct. All three together — a headache that is new to the patient, is getting worse, and does not remit.
Sudden and severe
A sudden, severe headache raises subarachnoid hemorrhage; a mass gives a new, progressive and persistent headache.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: In unilateral SENSORINEURAL loss, which way does the Weber sound lateralize?
opts: To the GOOD ear
Correct. Sound lateralizes to the good ear, because inner ear or cochlear nerve damage impairs transmission to the affected ear.
To the IMPAIRED ear, because the damage amplifies bone conduction
That is the conductive pattern, and damage does not amplify anything.
It does not lateralize in sensorineural loss
It does lateralize: in unilateral sensorineural loss the sound goes to the good ear, away from the damage.
It lateralizes to whichever ear was tested first
Which ear was tested first has no bearing on where the sound lateralizes.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Eye pain WITH BLINKING suggests what?
opts: Temporal arteritis
Temporal arteritis pairs eye pain with temporal pain; pain with blinking suggests a corneal abrasion or foreign body.
Corneal abrasion or a foreign body
Correct — eye pain with blinking points to a corneal abrasion or a foreign body on the eye's surface.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Acute narrow angle glaucoma pairs eye pain with headache; pain with blinking suggests corneal abrasion or foreign body.
Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis causes pain on eye motion; pain with blinking suggests a corneal abrasion or foreign body.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 17

E.io: h — Involving the patient in healthcare communication
E.q: How should communication style be handled across different patients?
opts: Keep communication strictly to the presenting clinical question
Communication is not restricted to one question; its style and content are adapted appropriately to each individual patient.
Adapt the style and content of communication appropriately for each patient
Correct — communication is expected to change to suit the patient rather than following one fixed script.
Use consistent phrasing with every patient so nothing is missed
Uniform phrasing is not the standard; a professional adapts the style and content of communication appropriately for each patient.
Match the register of whoever referred the patient
The referrer's register is irrelevant; communication style and content are adapted appropriately for each patient being seen.
E.cite: Intro to PD II - Elwaya .pdf, Page 23

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Insidious vertigo with hearing impaired on ONE side, tinnitus present, and possible cranial nerve V and VII involvement. Which is it?
opts: Acoustic neuroma compressing the vestibular branch of cranial nerve VIII
Correct. The unilateral hearing loss plus the neighboring cranial nerves is the signature — the tumor sits where V and VII run close by.
Ménière disease
Ménière is sudden and recurrent, and does not involve cranial nerves V and VII.
Central vertigo from a brainstem lesion
Hearing is NOT affected in central vertigo, and tinnitus is absent.
Drug toxicity
Drug toxicity impairs hearing bilaterally where it does so at all, and is linked to a specific agent.

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Why must the upper lid be everted in a corneal abrasion?
opts: To apply fluorescein more evenly
Fluorescein is simply placed in the eye and viewed under blue light; eversion is to find a foreign body under the upper lid.
To assess the tear film
The tear film is not the reason; eversion looks for a foreign body in the upper tarsal conjunctiva scratching the cornea.
A foreign body embedded in the upper tarsal conjunctiva can repeatedly scratch the cornea as the eye opens and closes
Correct — a foreign body embedded in the upper tarsal conjunctiva can scratch the cornea each time the eye opens and closes.
To measure the intraocular pressure accurately
Pressure is measured with a tonometer pen; eversion is to find a foreign body under the upper lid scratching the cornea.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 120

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
E.q: Which description fits a sunken eye from an orbital floor fracture?
opts: Photophobia and a dendrite — best seen with fluorescein
Fluorescein is taken up by corneal defects; a floor fracture shows ecchymosis, tenderness and a rim step-off, seen from above.
A red painless patch — best seen in ambient light
A painless red patch is a subconjunctival hemorrhage; a floor fracture shows ecchymosis, tenderness and a rim step-off.
Ecchymosis, point tenderness and a palpable step-off around the orbital rim — best observed from above the head looking down toward the eyes
Correct — a sunken eye with ecchymosis, point tenderness and a rim step-off suggests a floor fracture; look down from above the head.
Fever and purulent discharge — best observed with a slit lamp
Fever and purulent discharge suggest infection; a floor fracture shows ecchymosis, tenderness and a rim step-off, seen from above.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 115

E.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
E.q: Painful hemorrhagic vesicles on the tympanic membrane or canal. Which description fits?
opts: Tympanosclerosis with hemorrhage
Tympanosclerosis is a chalky hyaline deposit and is painless.
Bullous myringitis, viral or bacterial
Correct. Bullous myringitis gives painful hemorrhagic vesicles on the membrane or canal, and it may be viral or bacterial.
Bullous myringitis, which is always viral
It may be either viral or bacterial; the appearance does not settle it.
Otitis externa with secondary infection
Otitis externa gives a swollen tender canal, not hemorrhagic vesicles.

E.io: a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
E.q: Which gland secretes sweat in order to maintain body temperature?
opts: The sudoriferous (eccrine) gland
Correct — thermoregulatory sweating is the eccrine gland's job.
The apocrine gland
Apocrine glands become active at puberty and secrete pheromones rather than thermoregulatory sweat.
The sebaceous gland
Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, which keeps hair and skin moist.
The ceruminous gland
Cerumen is produced in the external ear canal and has no thermoregulatory role.
